claims.note: cBioPortal pdac_msk_2024 via API: KRAS-mutant 2,188 of 2,336 (93.7%), TP53 1,779 (76.2%), CDKN2A mutation or deep deletion 902 (38.6%), SMAD4 610 (26.1%); alleles G12D 40.3%, G12V 32.1%, G12R 16.0%, Q61 7.7%, G12C 1.3%. Singhi 2019: KRAS 88%. Hu 2018 5.5% and Shindo 2017 3.9% germline. Ranges hold for the cohorts in the molecular table.

claims.claim: Two survive every re-analysis, classical (GATA6-high) and basal-like or squamous (GATA6-low); in COMPASS basal-like tumours responded to first-line chemotherapy in 10% against 33% and lived 5.9 against 9.3 months, and a GATA6 in situ hybridisation stain calls the subtype with sensitivity 89% and specificity 83%.
claims.note: O'Kane 2020 (COMPASS): ORR "10% versus 33%"; "Median OS ... 9.3 months for classical versus 5.9 months for basal-like"; "ISH predicted the subtypes with sensitivity of 89% and specificity of 83%".

claims.claim: More than 99% of the smallest PanIN-1 lesions already carry KRAS, CDKN2A, GNAS or BRAF mutations, IPMNs carry GNAS R201 in 66%, and the classical KRAS-CDKN2A-TP53-SMAD4 ladder is only part of the story: two-thirds of genomes show punctuated rearrangements that knock out several drivers at once.
claims.note: Kanda 2012: "more than 99% of the earliest-stage, lowest-grade, pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasm-1 lesions contain mutations in KRAS, p16/CDKN2A, GNAS, or BRAF". Wu 2011: "GNAS mutations were present in 66% of IPMNs" (codon 201). Notta 2016: "Two-thirds of tumours harbour complex rearrangement patterns associated with mitotic errors".

claims.claim: CA 19-9 has pooled sensitivity 79% and specificity 82%, rises with cholestasis and cannot be made by the roughly 10% of patients who are Lewis-negative; ctDNA predicts recurrence about three months before imaging, but most assays read only KRAS codons 12, 13 and 61 and no approval uses it.
claims.note: Goonetilleke 2007: "pooled data from 2283 patients. The median sensitivity of CA 19-9 for diagnosis is 79 (70-90%) and median specificity 82 (68-91%)". The figures are medians across studies, not pooled estimates. Yeh 2026: Lewis-negative about 10%. Groot 2019: recurrence predicted with "median lead time of 84 days".
claims.fixed: "pooled sensitivity 79% and specificity 82%" to "a median sensitivity of 79% and specificity of 82% across studies" (card and the matching note on the same record)

claims.claim: CAPS surveillance of high-risk individuals shifted 57.9% of detected cancers to stage I (median survival 9.8 against 1.5 years); blood tests are not ready (the methylation test reads 16.8% sensitivity at stage I) and new-onset diabetes is the strongest clinical enrichment.
claims.note: Dbouk 2022: 57.9% stage I, median OS 9.8 against 1.5 years (correct). Klein 2021 (CCGA3): "stage I: 16.8%" is the sensitivity across all cancer types, not for pancreatic cancer, which a reader of this page would assume.
claims.fixed: "16.8% sensitivity at stage I" to "16.8% sensitivity at stage I across all cancers" (card and matching note)

claims.claim: Painless jaundice (yellow eyes or skin, dark urine, pale stools, itching) when a head-of-pancreas tumour blocks the bile duct; about 75 percent of cancers start in the head (Cancer Research UK)
claims.note: CRUK types page: "Roughly 75 out of 100 pancreatic cancers (roughly 75%) start in the head of the pancreas."

claims.claim: Get an urgent GP appointment or call NHS 111 for yellowing of the eyes or skin, vomiting for more than two days or diarrhoea for more than seven; see a GP for noticeable weight loss or symptoms that persist beyond two weeks (NHS)
claims.note: NHS symptoms page: urgent GP or 111 if "the whites of your eyes or your skin turn yellow", "being sick for more than 2 days", "diarrhoea for more than 7 days"; see a GP for "a noticeable amount of weight" lost or symptoms that "do not get better after 2 weeks".

claims.claim: Late diagnosis is the rule: 45 percent of English cases in 2019 were diagnosed after an emergency presentation and only 26 percent of staged cases in 2022 were stage I or II (Cancer Research UK); in the United States 51 percent are distant at diagnosis (SEER)
claims.note: CRUK summary: 2019 England "(45%) via an emergency presentation"; 2022 "26% ... with a known stage ... early stage (I & II)". SEER: distant 51%.

claims.claim: CA 19-9 is 79 to 81 percent sensitive and 82 to 90 percent specific in symptomatic patients, falsely negative in Lewis-negative people (5 to 10 percent) and raised by biliary obstruction and pancreatitis (Ballehaninna 2012)
claims.note: Ballehaninna 2012: "sensitivity and specificity of 79-81% and 82-90% ... in symptomatic patients"; "false negative results in Lewis negative phenotype (5-10%) and increased false positivity in the presence of obstructive jaundice".

claims.claim: EUS with fine-needle aspiration and cyst-fluid CEA when malignancy is in question; refer for resection with jaundice from a head cyst, an enhancing solid component or a main duct of 10 mm or more (NG85 1.1.7 to 1.1.13)
claims.note: NG85 1.1.9: refer for resection with "obstructive jaundice with cystic lesions in the head of the pancreas", "enhancing solid component", "a main pancreatic duct that is 10 mm diameter or larger"; 1.1.11-1.1.12 FNA with CEA.

claims.claim: Stage 1: T1 or T2, no nodes (1A, 1B).
claims.note: CRUK stage 1 page: 1A "T1, N0, M0"; 1B "T2, N0, M0".

claims.claim: Stage 2: T3 without nodes (2A) or T1 to T3 with one to three nodes (2B).
claims.note: CRUK TNM page: N1 "1 to 3 nearby lymph nodes"; stage 2A T3 N0, 2B T1-3 N1 per the same TNM grouping.

claims.claim: Stage 3: four or more nodes or a T4 tumour.
claims.note: CRUK stage 3 page: "spread to 4 or more nearby lymph nodes ... T1, N2, M0 ... Or ... T4, Any N, M0".

claims.claim: Stage 4: metastases, most often liver, peritoneum or lung (Cancer Research UK stages page)
claims.note: CRUK stages and stage 4 pages: "spread to other areas of the body, such as the liver or lungs". The page names no peritoneum and makes no "most often" ranking.
claims.fixed: "metastases, most often liver, peritoneum or lung" to "spread to other parts of the body, such as the liver or lungs"

claims.claim: Resectability decides treatment: resectable (no arterial contact, venous contact of 180 degrees or less without contour irregularity), borderline resectable (arterial contact under 180 degrees or reconstructable venous involvement; or a CA 19-9 above 500 U/mL, or suspected but unproven spread; or performance status 2 or worse) and locally advanced (arterial encasement or unreconstructable venous occlusion) (Isaji 2018;
claims.note: Isaji 2018: borderline anatomical contact "of less than 180°"; biological "CA 19-9 level more than 500 units/ml" or suspicious but unproven metastases; conditional "ECOG performance status of 2 or more".

claims.claim: UK staging tests: pancreatic protocol CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis for every new diagnosis (NG85 1.3.1);
claims.note: NG85 1.3.1: "offer a pancreatic protocol CT scan that includes the chest, abdomen and pelvis".

claims.claim: FDG PET-CT for localised disease before treatment (1.3.2);
claims.note: NG85 1.3.2: "Offer FDG-PET/CT to people with localised disease on CT who will be having cancer treatment".

claims.claim: In the United States 15 percent of cases are localised, 28 percent regional, 51 percent distant and 5 percent unstaged at diagnosis (SEER 21, 2016 to 2022)
claims.note: SEER: Localized 15%, Regional 28%, Distant 51%, Unknown 5%; "SEER 21 (Excluding IL) 2016–2022".

claims.claim: Emergency presentation: 45 percent of English cases (2019) and 60.9 percent of US Veterans Affairs cases (2026) are diagnosed as emergencies, with more advanced stage and higher mortality; the symptom-based referral rules (NG12) catch a minority.
claims.note: CRUK summary: England 2019 "(45%) via an emergency presentation". Khalaf, Br J Cancer 2026: "60.9% were identified as EPs"; more advanced stage (aOR 1.38) and higher mortality (aHR 1.64).

claims.claim: Enzyme replacement reaches a minority: only 21.7 percent of 4,554 UK patients in primary care records received pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy, and supplies were disrupted in 2024 (NG85 note), although it is a NICE recommendation for every unresectable patient.
claims.note: Roberts 2019: "PERT use among the whole cohort (987/4554) was 21.7%" (UK CPRD). NG85 1.6: "In September 2024, supplies of pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy were disrupted"; 1.6.1 "Offer enteric-coated pancreatin for people with unresectable pancreatic cancer."

claims.claim: The 1 mm margin rule is not used everywhere, so R0 and R1 rates and their survival differences are not comparable between series or trials (Strobel 2017).
claims.note: Strobel 2017: "The strict definition of R0 requiring a 1 mm tumor-free margin is not commonly accepted. Reported R0/R1 rates and associated survival are highly heterogeneous"; "vary significantly with the definitions used".

claims.claim: Neither the new-onset diabetes score (3.6 percent prevalence among high scorers) nor carrier surveillance (7 of 9 CAPS5 cancers at stage I) has been tested prospectively at population scale, and CA 19-9 cannot be read in the Lewis-negative tenth of patients; four in five patients still present with disease that cannot be removed.
claims.note: Sharma 2018 3.6% and Dbouk 2022 7 of 9 CAPS5 stage I hold; Lewis-negative about a tenth holds (Yeh 2026 "∼10%"). "Four in five patients still present with disease that cannot be removed" has no source on the record (SEER gives 15% localised, a different measure).
claims.fixed: "four in five patients still present" to "most patients still present"

claims.claim: Enzyme replacement reached 21.7 percent of UK patients in primary care data and cachexia has a mechanism-based drug in phase 2 but no phase 3; both determine whether combination chemotherapy is delivered, and both sit outside the trials that set the standards.
claims.note: Roberts 2019: 21.7% PERT use (correct). "Cachexia has a mechanism-based drug in phase 2 but no phase 3" is contradicted by ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06989437: "A Phase 2b/3, Randomized, Double-Blind Study ... Ponsegromab ... Cachexia and Metastatic Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma", recruiting since 3 October 2025 (the record's own trial list includes it).
claims.fixed: "a mechanism-based drug in phase 2 but no phase 3" to "a mechanism-based drug (ponsegromab) only in a phase 2/3 trial that has not reported (NCT06989437)"

claims.claim: Alliance A021806 (primary completion December 2028) and PREOPANC-3 are the only trials comparing perioperative chemotherapy with the current adjuvant standard, and until they read out neoadjuvant treatment for clearly resectable disease rests on secondary endpoints.
claims.note: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04340141 (Alliance A021806): primary completion 2028-12-31 (estimated), active not recruiting, 358 enrolled.

claims.claim: Supportive treatments that most patients need, enzyme replacement, coeliac plexus block, stents and cachexia drugs, rest on small or observational studies; the one randomised trial of enzyme replacement was negative on its primary endpoint, cachexia has a mechanism-based drug (ponsegromab) in phase 2 but no phase 3, and both sit outside the trials that set the standards even though they decide whether combination chemotherapy is delivered.
claims.note: "Ponsegromab in phase 2 but no phase 3" is contradicted by ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06989437, a phase 2b/3 ponsegromab trial in cachexia with metastatic PDAC, recruiting since 3 October 2025 and listed in this record's own trials.
claims.fixed: "(ponsegromab) in phase 2 but no phase 3" to "(ponsegromab) only in a phase 2/3 trial that has not reported (NCT06989437)"

claims.claim: CA 19-9 cannot be produced by about a tenth of patients, whose outlook is as poor as the highest-marker group, so a normal marker is a false reassurance that no guideline yet corrects with Lewis genotyping.
claims.note: Yeh 2026: Lewis-negative "∼10%"; FUT3-null median OS 13.5 months "comparable" to CA19-9 >200 U/mL (12.9 months).

claims.claim: Resectable / borderline: Neoadjuvant mFOLFIRINOX (borderline; increasingly resectable), surgery, then adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX to complete ~6 months (PRODIGE 24); gemcitabine/capecitabine if unfit.
claims.note: PRODIGE 24 (Conroy, NEJM 2018): modified FOLFIRINOX "for 24 weeks" after resection (about 6 months); gemcitabine plus capecitabine for the less fit matches NG85 1.8.6. No other figure.

claims.claim: RASolute 302: OS 13.2 vs 6.7 months, HR 0.40); otherwise switch backbone (gem/nab-pac after FOLFIRINOX, or liposomal irinotecan/5-FU after gemcitabine).
claims.note: FDA notice for daraxonrasib (RASolute 302): median OS 13.2 against 6.7 months, hazard ratio 0.40.

claims.claim: Borderline resectable (the tumour touches a main vein or artery, so an operation straight away would probably leave cancer behind): chemotherapy first for two to four months, usually modified FOLFIRINOX, then restaging, with surgery about 6 to 8 weeks after chemotherapy if the disease has not spread;
claims.note: "Two to four months" matches the cited trials: ESPAC-5 (row ref) gave two 28-day cycles of GemCap or four 2-weekly cycles of FOLFIRINOX (8 weeks), and A021501 (on this record) 8 two-weekly cycles (16 weeks). "Surgery about 6 to 8 weeks after chemotherapy" was not on any page linked on the record. Pancreatic Cancer UK "who can have surgery" page: "The operation will usually happen around 6–8 weeks after you finish chemotherapy, although this can vary."
claims.fixed: Added the Pancreatic Cancer UK "who can have surgery" page to the record's links; text unchanged

claims.claim: In the Dutch PREOPANC trial, chemoradiotherapy before surgery improved five-year survival over surgery first (20.5% against 6.5%), most clearly for borderline disease; the record's open problems note the question is unresolved for resectable disease after PREOPANC-2, NORPACT-1 and Alliance A021806.
claims.note: Versteijne, JCO 2022 (PREOPANC long-term): 5-year OS "20.5% ... with neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy and 6.5% ... with upfront surgery"; "The effect of neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy was consistent across the prespecified subgroups, including resectable and borderline resectable". "Most clearly for borderline disease" is not what the long-term report says.
claims.fixed: "most clearly for borderline disease" to "with the same effect in resectable and borderline disease"

claims.claim: FOLFIRINOX (fluorouracil, folinic acid, irinotecan and oxaliplatin, every two weeks with a 46-hour pump): NICE NG85 offers it to people with metastatic disease and a performance status of 0 to 1; in the 2011 trial median survival was 11.1 months against 6.8 with gemcitabine, with more diarrhoea, neuropathy and low blood counts, so most UK units give the modified doses.
claims.note: NG85 1.9.4: "Offer FOLFIRINOX to people with metastatic pancreatic cancer and an ... ECOG performance status of 0 to 1". Conroy, NEJM 2011: "median overall survival was 11.1 months ... as compared with 6.8 months".

claims.claim: Gemcitabine with nab-paclitaxel (weekly drips for three weeks in four): improved survival over gemcitabine alone in MPACT (8.5 against 6.7 months) and causes hair loss, neuropathy and low counts;
claims.note: Von Hoff, NEJM 2013 (MPACT): "median overall survival was 8.5 months ... as compared with 6.7 months"; grade 3+ neuropathy and neutropenia more common.

claims.claim: NALIRIFOX (liposomal irinotecan, oxaliplatin, fluorouracil): in NAPOLI 3 median survival was 11.1 months against 9.2 with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel; it is on the OnCo record beside modified FOLFIRINOX for fit patients but NHS funding follows NICE appraisals, so ask what applies where you are treated.
claims.note: Wainberg, Lancet 2023 (NAPOLI 3): "Median overall survival was 11·1 months ... with NALIRIFOX versus 9·2 months ... with nab-paclitaxel-gemcitabine".

claims.claim: Everyone has a DPD blood test before fluorouracil or capecitabine, blood counts before each dose, scans about every three months, and the same temperature rule for the 24-hour line.
claims.note: CRUK chemotherapy page supports the DPD test before capecitabine or fluorouracil. "Scans about every three months" is on no page linked on the record; Pancreatic Cancer UK says "You will have scans before, during and at the end of your treatment to see how the chemotherapy is working".
claims.fixed: "scans about every three months" to "scans before, during and at the end of treatment" (Pancreatic Cancer UK wording)

claims.claim: NICE NG85 says start once you have had time to recover and as soon as you are well enough to tolerate all six cycles, offers gemcitabine plus capecitabine (GemCap, from ESPAC-4: median survival 28.0 months against 25.5 with gemcitabine alone) and considers gemcitabine alone for those not well enough for a combination; since PRODIGE 24 (2018), modified FOLFIRINOX has become the standard for fit patients, with a median survival of 54.4 months against 35.0 with gemcitabine in the 2018 report (53.5 against 35.5 months at the five-year update in 2022), at the cost of more diarrhoea, neuropathy and tiredness, and Pancreatic Cancer UK lists all three as the options, chosen by how well you are.
claims.note: NG85 1.8.5 "as soon as they are well enough to tolerate all 6 cycles"; 1.8.6 offer gemcitabine plus capecitabine; 1.8.7 consider gemcitabine. ESPAC-4: 28.0 against 25.5 months. PRODIGE 24: 54.4 against 35.0 months (NEJM 2018); 53.5 against 35.5 months (JAMA Oncol 2022).

claims.claim: Cancer Research UK and Pancreatic Cancer UK say it should start within 12 weeks (3 months) of surgery and lasts up to 6 months, so sorting out eating, weight, enzyme doses and blood sugar in the weeks after the operation matters: they are the usual reasons for a delay.
claims.note: Pancreatic Cancer UK: "you need to be well enough for six months of chemotherapy. Your chemotherapy should begin in the first 12 weeks after your surgery"; CRUK: "It should start within 3 months of having surgery ... for up to 6 months".

claims.claim: Follow-up after chemotherapy is usually a CT scan every 6 months for 5 years with blood tests and sometimes CA 19-9; contact the team about any new symptom between visits.
claims.note: CRUK follow-up page: "If all is well, you usually then have CT scans every 6 months for 5 years."

claims.claim: Treatment: platinum chemotherapy (FOLFIRINOX or NALIRIFOX, which contain oxaliplatin) is favoured, and in the POLO trial maintenance olaparib after at least 16 weeks of platinum without progression lengthened the time before the cancer grew (7.4 against 3.8 months) without lengthening survival overall;
claims.note: Golan, NEJM 2019 (POLO): after at least 16 weeks of platinum, "median progression-free survival ... (7.4 months vs. 3.8 months ...)"; final OS (Kindler, JCO 2022) "No statistically significant OS benefit".

claims.claim: NICE could not make a recommendation on olaparib in pancreatic cancer (TA750, terminated December 2021) because the company made no submission, so ask what is funded where you are treated.
claims.note: NICE TA750 page: "Terminated: 8 December 2021"; "NICE is unable to make a recommendation on olaparib".

claims.claim: Family: Macmillan says each child of a carrier has a 1 in 2 chance of inheriting the variant; the genetics team can offer relatives predictive testing, and NICE NG85 says offer pancreatic surveillance (MRI/MRCP or EUS) to people with BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2 or CDKN2A variants who have a first-degree relative with pancreatic cancer, and to those with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome or hereditary pancreatitis.
claims.note: Macmillan BRCA page: "a 1 in 2 (50%) chance of passing the variant to each of their children". NG85 1.1.15 to 1.1.17 surveillance criteria as stated.

claims.claim: Macmillan describes the injection through the back or from inside the stomach during an endoscopic ultrasound, and a randomised trial (Wyse 2011) found early EUS-guided neurolysis reduced pain at three months.
claims.note: Wyse, JCO 2011: early EUS-guided coeliac plexus neurolysis, pain relief "significantly greater at 3 months"; "no effect on QOL or survival".

claims.claim: How to take it: with all meals, snacks and milky drinks, half with the first mouthfuls and half spread through the meal, swallowed with a cool drink, starting at about 50,000 to 75,000 units for a main meal and 25,000 to 50,000 for a snack, more for larger or fattier meals, reviewed by the dietitian and increased until symptoms settle; if it is not working, a proton pump inhibitor, another brand, or another cause (bile acid diarrhoea, bacterial overgrowth, medicines) is looked for.
claims.note: Pancreatic Cancer UK PERT page: "Take half the capsules with the first few mouthfuls of food. Spread the other half out during the meal"; "start with a dose of at least 50,000 or 75,000 units for a main meal, and 25,000 or 50,000 units for a snack or milky drink".

claims.claim: Diabetes: pancreatic cancer or surgery can cause type 3c diabetes, which differs from type 1 and 2, usually needs tablets or insulin, and is managed by a diabetes nurse and specialist dietitian who know you have pancreatic cancer; a systematic review found new diabetes in about 16 in 100 people after a Whipple operation, and removing the whole pancreas means insulin for life.
claims.note: Scholten, Surgery 2018: "The mean weighted overall proportion of new-onset diabetes mellitus after pancreatoduodenectomy was 16%".

claims.claim: Pancreatic Cancer UK says these services are not just for the end of life and are available at any point for cancer that cannot be cured, and a randomised trial (Temel 2010) found early palliative care alongside cancer treatment improved quality of life and mood.
claims.note: Temel, NEJM 2010 is "Early palliative care for patients with metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer": better quality of life and fewer depressive symptoms. It was not linked on the record, and the sentence on a pancreatic page did not say it was a lung cancer trial.
claims.fixed: "a randomised trial (Temel 2010)" to "a randomised trial in advanced lung cancer (Temel 2010)"; Temel 2010 added to the record's links

claims.claim: Resectable disease: upfront surgery or neoadjuvant treatment: Upfront pancreatoduodenectomy or distal pancreatectomy followed by six months of adjuvant chemotherapy remains the reference for clearly resectable tumours: NORPACT-1 found 18-month survival 60 percent with neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX against 73 percent with surgery first, SWOG S1505 found two-year survival of 47 to 48 percent with either perioperative regimen (no better than adjuvant history), and NEONAX missed its 18-month disease-free target in both arms.
claims.note: NORPACT-1 (Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2024): alive at 18 months by ITT "60% ... versus 73%". SWOG S1505 (JAMA Oncol 2021): "Two-year OS was 47% ... and 48%", neither above the historical threshold. NEONAX (Ann Oncol 2023): "The pre-defined DFS rate of 55% at 18 months was not reached in both arms".

claims.claim: In favour of treating first: PREOPANC-1's neoadjuvant gemcitabine chemoradiotherapy gave five-year survival 20.5 against 6.5 percent (hazard ratio 0.73) across resectable and borderline patients, and PREOPANC-2 found neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX and neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy equivalent (21.9 against 21.3 months).
claims.note: PREOPANC long-term: 20.5% against 6.5%, HR 0.73 (correct). PREOPANC-2 (Lancet Oncol 2025): 21.9 against 21.3 months, HR 0.88, p=0.32; "did not show a difference in overall survival". It was not an equivalence trial, so "equivalent" overstated it.
claims.fixed: "found neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX and neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy equivalent" to "found no survival difference between neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX and neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy"

claims.claim: Alliance A021806 (358 patients, perioperative against adjuvant modified FOLFIRINOX, primary completion December 2028) and PREOPANC-3 (378 patients) will settle the question;
claims.note: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04340141 (Alliance A021806): 358 actual, primary completion 2028-12-31. NCT04927780 (PREOPANC-3): enrolment 378 (estimated), active not recruiting.

claims.claim: Adjuvant chemotherapy after resection: Modified FOLFIRINOX for six months in fit patients (PRODIGE 24: median overall survival 53.5 against 35.5 months with gemcitabine, hazard ratio 0.68, five-year survival 43.2 against 31.4 percent).
claims.note: Conroy, JAMA Oncol 2022: median OS 53.5 against 35.5 months, HR 0.68; 5-year OS 43.2% against 31.4%.

claims.claim: Gemcitabine plus capecitabine for those not eligible (ESPAC-4: 28.0 against 25.5 months, hazard ratio 0.82; long-term 31.6 against 28.4 months, and 49.9 against 32.2 months after R0 resection); this is the NICE NG85 recommendation for England (1.8.6, off-label).
claims.note: ESPAC-4 (Lancet 2017): 28.0 against 25.5 months, HR 0.82. Long-term (JCO 2025): 31.6 against 28.4 months; R0 49.9 against 32.2 months. NG85 1.8.6: "Offer adjuvant gemcitabine plus capecitabine ... In February 2018, this was an off-label use."

claims.claim: Gemcitabine alone for the frail (CONKO-001: five-year survival 20.7 against 10.4 percent with observation;
claims.note: Oettle, JAMA 2013 (CONKO-001): "5-year overall survival of 20.7% ... vs 10.4%".

claims.claim: S-1 for six months in Japan (JASPAC 01: five-year survival 44.1 against 24.4 percent with gemcitabine, hazard ratio 0.57), not licensed for this use in Europe.
claims.note: Uesaka, Lancet 2016 (JASPAC 01): "HR of mortality was 0.57 ... 5-year overall survival of 24.4% ... in the gemcitabine group and 44.1% ... in the S-1 group".

claims.claim: Borderline resectable disease: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy for two to four months, then restaging and surgery: ESPAC-5 (90 patients, UK and Germany) found one-year survival 39 percent with immediate surgery against 78 percent after gemcitabine plus capecitabine, 84 percent after FOLFIRINOX and 60 percent after chemoradiotherapy.
claims.note: ESPAC-5 (Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2023): 90 randomised, 16 centres "in two countries (UK and Germany)"; "1-year overall survival was 39% ... for immediate surgery, 78% ... gemcitabine plus capecitabine, 84% ... FOLFIRINOX, and 60% ... chemoradiotherapy". Short courses were 8 weeks; A021501 16 weeks, so two to four months holds.

claims.claim: Alliance A021501 established modified FOLFIRINOX alone as the reference regimen (18-month survival 66.7 percent, median 29.8 months) after its stereotactic radiotherapy arm closed at interim analysis for fewer R0 resections (10 against 17 of the first 30).
claims.note: Katz, JAMA Oncol 2022 (A021501): "Among the first 30 evaluable patients ... 17 ... (57%) and 10 ... (33%) had undergone R0 resection, leading to closure of arm 2"; arm 1 18-month OS 66.7%, median 29.8 months.

claims.claim: Locally advanced unresectable disease: chemotherapy, chemoradiation, stereotactic radiotherapy and ablation: Four to six months of modified FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel (NEOLAP: conversion to resection in 36 to 44 percent of randomised patients with either sequence, median survival 18.5 to 20.7 months).
claims.note: NEOLAP (Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2021): "surgical conversion rate of 35·9% ... and 43·9%"; "median overall survival was 18·5 months ... and 20·7 months". LAP07 used 4 months of induction.

claims.claim: Chemoradiotherapy after induction improves local control but not survival: LAP07 (15.2 against 16.5 months; local progression 32 against 46 percent), CONKO-007 (R0 resection 25 against 18 percent overall, not significant;
claims.note: LAP07 (JAMA 2016): OS "chemotherapy at 16.5 months ... and chemoradiotherapy at 15.2 months"; "decreased local progression (32% vs 46%". CONKO-007 (JCO 2025): R0 "25% (43 of 169) ... versus 18%", P = .113.

claims.claim: 69 against 50 percent among those operated; survival hazard ratio 0.94).
claims.note: CONKO-007: R0 among those operated "69.4% (43 of 62) compared with ... 50.0%"; "No difference in OS ... (hazard ratio [HR], 0.937".

claims.claim: When it is used, capecitabine is the radiosensitiser (SCALOP: median survival 15.2 against 13.4 months with gemcitabine;
claims.note: SCALOP (Lancet Oncol 2013): "Median overall survival was 15·2 months ... in the capecitabine group and 13·4 months ... in the gemcitabine group". NG85 1.9.3: "consider capecitabine as the radiosensitiser".

claims.claim: Stereotactic radiotherapy and irreversible electroporation are options in centres with experience: CROSSFIRE (68 patients after FOLFIRINOX) found MRI-guided stereotactic radiotherapy and electroporation equivalent (16.1 against 12.5 months, hazard ratio 1.39, stopped for futility), and PANFIRE-2 (50 patients) reported median survival 17 months from diagnosis with major complications in 42 percent.
claims.note: CROSSFIRE (Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2024): 68 patients, OS 16·1 against 12·5 months, HR 1·39, accrual "stopped early for futility"; "did not identify a difference", which is not a demonstration of equivalence. PANFIRE-2 (Radiology 2020): 50 participants, median OS 17 months from diagnosis; "Fourteen minor and 21 major complications occurred in 29 of the 50 participants (58%)". 42 percent was 21 complications divided by 50 people, not the share of patients with a major complication.
claims.fixed: "found ... equivalent" to "found no survival difference between"; "major complications in 42 percent" to "21 major complications among the 50 participants"

claims.claim: Metastatic disease, first line: FOLFIRINOX for performance status 0 to 1 (PRODIGE 4/ACCORD 11: median overall survival 11.1 against 6.8 months with gemcitabine, hazard ratio 0.57; febrile neutropenia 5.4 percent) or NALIRIFOX (NAPOLI 3: 11.1 against 9.2 months with nab-paclitaxel and gemcitabine, hazard ratio 0.83 in the Lancet report and 0.84 on the Onivyde label;
claims.note: PRODIGE 4 (NEJM 2011): 11.1 against 6.8 months, HR 0.57, febrile neutropenia 5.4%. NAPOLI 3 (Lancet 2023): 11·1 against 9·2 months, HR 0·83. Onivyde label (openFDA) Table 8: "Hazard Ratio (95% CI) 0.84 (0.71, 0.99)". FDA approval 13 February 2024 (Drugs@FDA supplement 16, 20240213); NICE TA1052 "Terminated: 2 April 2025".

claims.claim: Gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel for those less fit or with biliary stents (MPACT: 8.5 against 6.7 months, hazard ratio 0.72; grade 3 or worse neuropathy 17 percent); in England only when other combinations are unsuitable (NICE TA476).
claims.note: MPACT (NEJM 2013): 8.5 against 6.7 months, HR 0.72; grade 3+ "neuropathy (17% vs. 1%)". NICE TA476 1.1: recommended "only if: other combination chemotherapies are unsuitable".

claims.claim: Four months of FOLFIRINOX then fluorouracil and leucovorin maintenance is an alternative to six months (PANOPTIMOX-PRODIGE 35: six-month progression-free survival 42.9 against 47.1 percent, survival without quality-of-life deterioration 11.4 against 7.2 months).
claims.note: PANOPTIMOX-PRODIGE 35 (JCO 2021): 6-month PFS "47.1% in A, 42.9% in B"; survival without QoL deterioration "maintenance arm (11.4 months) than in arms A and C (7.2 and 7.5 months".

claims.claim: Metastatic disease, second line: Daraxonrasib after one prior line (RASolute 302: median overall survival 13.2 against 6.7 months with chemotherapy, hazard ratio 0.40; progression-free 7.2 against 3.6 months;
claims.note: RASolute 302 (NEJM 2026): overall population OS 13.2 against 6.7 months, HR 0.40; PFS 7.2 against 3.6 months.

claims.claim: FDA approval 26 August 2026 for metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma after one systemic therapy or for people not fit for multi-agent chemotherapy; no EU or UK decision).
claims.note: FDA notice: approved August 26, 2026 for adults with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma after at least one prior systemic therapy or not candidates for multiagent therapy.

claims.claim: Otherwise switch backbone: after gemcitabine, liposomal irinotecan with fluorouracil and leucovorin (NAPOLI-1: 6.1 against 4.2 months, hazard ratio 0.67;
claims.note: NAPOLI-1 (Lancet 2016): "6.1 months ... vs 4.2 months ... (hazard ratio 0.67".

claims.claim: FDA 2015, EU 2016, not recommended by NICE TA440) or OFF (CONKO-003: 5.9 against 3.3 months, hazard ratio 0.66), noting that PANCREOX found modified FOLFOX6 worse than fluorouracil alone; after FOLFIRINOX, gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel.
claims.note: Drugs@FDA Onivyde original approval 20151022; EMA: "marketing authorisation valid throughout the EU on 14 October 2016"; NICE TA440 1.1 "not recommended". CONKO-003 (JCO 2014): OFF 5.9 against 3.3 months, HR 0.66.

claims.claim: NG85 recommends oxaliplatin-based or gemcitabine-based second line (1.9.7, 1.9.8).
claims.note: NG85 1.9.7 "Consider oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy as second-line"; 1.9.8 "Consider gemcitabine-based chemotherapy ... after first-line FOLFIRINOX".

claims.claim: Maintenance after first-line platinum: germline BRCA carriers: Olaparib 300 mg twice daily for people with a germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation whose metastatic disease has not progressed after at least 16 weeks of platinum chemotherapy (POLO: progression-free survival 7.4 against 3.8 months, hazard ratio 0.53; overall survival 19.0 against 19.2 months, hazard ratio 0.83, not significant; three-year survival 33.9 against 17.8 percent;
claims.note: POLO (NEJM 2019): ≥16 weeks platinum, PFS 7.4 against 3.8 months, HR 0.53. Final OS (Kindler, JCO 2022): "median 19.0 v 19.2 months; hazard ratio [HR], 0.83", 3-year 33.9% against 17.8%; olaparib 300 mg twice daily. TA750 terminated 8 December 2021.

claims.claim: About 2 to 3 percent of unselected patients carry a germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 variant (Hu 2018, 3,030 patients: BRCA2 1.9 percent, BRCA1 0.6 percent), more in familial disease;
claims.note: Hu 2018: BRCA2 1.9% and BRCA1 0.6% of 3,030 cases (2.5% together, so about 2 to 3 percent).

claims.claim: 7.5 percent of the 3,315 screened for POLO carried one and 154 were randomised.
claims.note: POLO full text (PMC6810605): "A total of 3315 patients were screened for trial entry; 247 (7.5%) of these patients had a germ-line BRCA mutation"; 154 randomised.

claims.claim: Targeted and biomarker-directed therapy: RAS: daraxonrasib works across RAS G12 mutations (91.8 percent of RASolute 302) and is approved regardless of subtype;
claims.note: RASolute 302 (NEJM 2026): "A total of 500 patients, including 91.8% with RAS G12 mutations"; FDA indication carries no mutation restriction.

claims.claim: KRAS G12C (1 to 2 percent of tumours) responds to sotorasib (CodeBreaK 100 pancreatic cohort, 38 patients: response 21 percent, median survival 6.9 months) and adagrasib (KRYSTAL-1: 7 of 21 responses), which NCCN lists but no regulator has approved for pancreatic cancer;
claims.note: CodeBreaK 100 (NEJM 2023): 38 patients, "8 patients had a centrally confirmed objective response (21%", median OS 6.9 months. KRYSTAL-1 (JCO 2023): "7/21 (33.3%) responses in pancreatic". G12C share 1.3% in cBioPortal pdac_msk_2024.

claims.claim: KRAS G12D (about 40 percent) has zoldonrasib in phase 3 first line (RASolute 305 with chemotherapy, RASolute 309 with daraxonrasib) after MRTX1133 was stopped.
claims.note: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT07621718 "RASolute 305" zoldonrasib plus chemotherapy, first line, phase 3; NCT07805954 "RASolute 309" zoldonrasib plus daraxonrasib, first line, phase 3; NCT05737706 MRTX1133 "TERMINATED", why stopped "Formulation challenges". G12D 40.3% of KRAS mutations in cBioPortal pdac_msk_2024.

claims.claim: NRG1 fusions (KRAS wild-type tumours): zenocutuzumab (eNRGy: response 42 percent in 36 pancreatic patients;
claims.note: Schram, NEJM 2025 (eNRGy): "15 of 36 patients (42% ...) with pancreatic cancer". (The Bizengri label's primary set reads 40% of 30.)

claims.claim: FDA accelerated approval 4 December 2024; not authorised in the EU).
claims.note: Drugs@FDA (openFDA) Bizengri: "ORIG 1 20241204 Type 1 - New Molecular Entity". The FDA notice URL now returns "Page Not Found".

claims.claim: Mismatch repair deficiency (about 1 percent): pembrolizumab (KEYNOTE-158 pancreatic cohort: 4 of 22 responses, 18 percent) or dostarlimab under tumour-agnostic US approvals;
claims.note: KEYNOTE-158 (Marabelle, JCO 2020) abstract gives only the pooled ORR 34.3%; the per-tumour table (pancreatic 22 patients, 4 responses) is an image in the PMC full text (PMC8184060), and the Europe PMC full-text XML returned HTTP 500. The about 1 percent dMMR share is consistent with the molecular table (0.5 to 2%).

claims.claim: Tumour treating fields for locally advanced disease: Alternating electric fields at 150 kHz worn for at least 18 hours a day through skin arrays, with gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel (PANOVA-3, 571 patients: median overall survival 16.2 against 14.2 months, hazard ratio 0.82; pain-free survival 15.2 against 9.1 months; progression-free survival, local control and response not improved; device-related skin events in 76.3 percent, grade 3 in 7.7 percent).
claims.note: PANOVA-3 (JCO 2025): 571 patients; OS 16.2 against 14.2 months, HR 0.82; pain-free survival 15.2 against 9.1 months; "PFS, local PFS, and ORR were not improved"; skin AEs 76.3%, grade 3 7.7%. Full text (PMC13472160): "TTFields therapy (150 kHz) ... recommended average usage of ≥75% (≥18 hours/day)".

claims.claim: Vaccines and cellular therapy: trials only: Personalised mRNA neoantigen vaccine: in the 16-patient phase 1, autogene cevumeran after surgery with atezolizumab and modified FOLFIRINOX induced T cells in 8, whose recurrence-free survival was not reached against 13.4 months in non-responders at 3.2 years, with vaccine-induced T cell clones estimated to live 7.7 years; the randomised phase 2 IMCODE003 (260 patients, eight UK sites) is closed to recruitment with disease-free survival due in 2031.
claims.note: Sethna, Nature 2025: 3.2-year median follow-up, responders (n = 8) RFS not reached against 13.4 months in non-responders (n = 8), clone lifespan 7.7 years. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05968326 (IMCODE003): phase 2, 260 estimated, active not recruiting, primary completion 2031-01-01, 8 UK locations of 87.

claims.claim: UK access to treatments (NICE, September 2026): Commissioned in England: FOLFIRINOX first line for performance status 0 to 1 and gemcitabine combinations or gemcitabine alone otherwise (NG85 1.9.4 to 1.9.6, several off-label); nab-paclitaxel with gemcitabine only when other combinations are unsuitable (TA476); adjuvant gemcitabine plus capecitabine or gemcitabine (NG85 1.8.6, 1.8.7); oxaliplatin-based or gemcitabine-based second line (1.9.7, 1.9.8); larotrectinib for NTRK fusions through the Cancer Drugs Fund (TA630).
claims.note: NG85 1.9.4 to 1.9.6 (FOLFIRINOX for ECOG 0 to 1, gemcitabine combinations, gemcitabine; off-label notes), 1.8.6 and 1.8.7, 1.9.7 and 1.9.8 read in raw text; TA476 1.1 "only if: other combination chemotherapies are unsuitable".

claims.claim: Terminated without a recommendation because the company made no submission: olaparib maintenance for germline BRCA carriers (TA750, December 2021) and NALIRIFOX (TA1052, April 2025).
claims.note: NICE TA750 "Terminated: 8 December 2021"; TA1052 "Terminated: 2 April 2025", both "unable to make a recommendation".

claims.claim: Palliation: biliary and duodenal obstruction: Self-expanding metal stent by ERCP for jaundice in unresectable disease and, when drainage is needed before surgery, in resectable disease (NG85 1.7.3 to 1.7.5); metal stents stay open 4.45 months longer than plastic with fewer cholangitis episodes and re-interventions (Almadi 2017, 20 trials).
claims.note: NG85 1.7.3 to 1.7.5 (self-expanding metal stents). Almadi 2017: "20 RCTs ... time to stent patency (4 studies) of 4.45 months ... favoring SEMS"; fewer sepsis or cholangitis and re-interventions.

claims.claim: Surgery first rather than preoperative drainage in fit resectable patients (1.7.1).
claims.note: NG85 1.7.1: "Offer resectional surgery rather than preoperative biliary drainage to people who: have resectable pancreatic cancer and obstructive jaundice and are well enough".

claims.claim: For duodenal obstruction, an enteral stent relieves symptoms within days and gastrojejunostomy lasts longer (SUSTENT); choose bypass for people with a better prognosis (1.7.8) and consider prophylactic gastrojejunostomy when a tumour is found unresectable at operation (1.7.6).
claims.note: SUSTENT (GIE 2010): food intake improved faster after stent (median 5 against 8 days) but long-term relief better after gastrojejunostomy. NG85 1.7.6 prophylactic gastrojejunostomy if unresectable at operation; 1.7.8 gastrojejunostomy for a more favourable prognosis.

claims.claim: Wyse 2011 randomised trial: pain scores lower at three months, no survival effect); no thoracic splanchnicectomy (1.5.2).
claims.note: Wyse 2011: pain relief "significantly greater at 3 months"; "no effect on QOL or survival". NG85 1.5.2: "Do not offer thoracic splanchnicectomy".

claims.claim: Thromboprophylaxis is decided by risk score under the NICE venous thromboembolism guideline; in CASSINI's pancreatic subgroup rivaroxaban cut clots during treatment (3.7 against 10.1 percent) but not over 180 days.
claims.note: CASSINI pancreatic subgroup (Cancer Med 2020): intervention period "5/135 (3.7%) ... rivaroxaban and 14/138 (10.1%) ... placebo"; up to day 180 HR 0.70, P = .328.

claims.claim: Gemcitabine became the standard in 1997 by improving symptoms and survival modestly over fluorouracil.
claims.note: Burris, JCO 1997 (a keyPaper of this record): clinical benefit 23.8% against 4.8%, median survival 5.65 against 4.41 months over 5-FU.

claims.claim: Two combinations then beat it: FOLFIRINOX in PRODIGE 4/ACCORD 11 (2011) for fit patients, and gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel in MPACT (2013) for a broader group.
claims.note: Conroy, NEJM 2011 (PRODIGE 4/ACCORD 11) and Von Hoff, NEJM 2013 (MPACT), both keyPapers of this record.

claims.claim: The field changed in 2026 when RASolute 302 showed that daraxonrasib, an inhibitor of the active form of all RAS proteins, lengthened survival over chemotherapy after first-line treatment; it is now approved and is being tested first line with and without chemotherapy and in the adjuvant setting.
claims.note: RASolute 302 (NEJM 2026) and FDA approval 26 August 2026; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07491445 "RASolute 303" first-line daraxonrasib with or without gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel, phase 3; NCT07252232 "RASolute 304" resected PDAC, phase 3.

claims.claim: G12D-selective inhibitors (zoldonrasib, MRTX1133 and others) are in phase 3 first line, G12C inhibitors are used off label or in trials for the small G12C group, and shared KRAS vaccines, personalised mRNA vaccines, claudin 18.2 and mesothelin-directed antibodies, antibody-drug conjugates and CAR-T cells are in trials.
claims.note: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05737706 (MRTX1133, the record's own pipeline trial): phase 1, "TERMINATED", why stopped "Formulation challenges", primary completion 2025-03-10. MRTX1133 is not in phase 3. Zoldonrasib is (RASolute 305, 309).
claims.fixed: "G12D-selective inhibitors (zoldonrasib, MRTX1133 and others) are in phase 3 first line" to "The G12D-selective inhibitor zoldonrasib is in phase 3 first line (MRTX1133 was stopped in phase 1)"

claims.claim: Three combination regimens lengthen life first line and NALIRIFOX is the newest (NAPOLI 3, approved 2024).
claims.note: Drugs@FDA Onivyde efficacy supplement 16 approved 20240213 (NALIRIFOX, NAPOLI 3); FDA notice "On February 13, 2024, the Food and Drug Administration approved irinotecan liposome ... with oxaliplatin, fluorouracil, and leucovorin".

claims.claim: Daraxonrasib is the first RAS inhibitor to lengthen survival in pancreatic cancer (RASolute 302, 2026) and is approved after first-line chemotherapy.
claims.note: RASolute 302 (NEJM 2026) overall survival 13.2 against 6.7 months; FDA approval 26 August 2026 after prior systemic therapy.

claims.claim: Surgery alone cures few patients: CONKO-001 (2007) showed that adjuvant gemcitabine roughly doubles the number alive without recurrence, ESPAC-4 (2017) that gemcitabine plus capecitabine does better, and PRODIGE 24 (2018) that six months of modified FOLFIRINOX after surgery gives the longest survival yet seen in the disease for patients fit enough to receive it.
claims.note: CONKO-001 (Oettle; long-term JAMA 2013 report of the trial first published 2007): median DFS 13.4 against 6.7 months, roughly double. ESPAC-4 Lancet 2017; PRODIGE 24 NEJM 2018 with median OS 54.4 months, the longest in a pancreatic trial on this record.

claims.claim: Whether upfront chemotherapy helps clearly resectable tumours is not settled: PREOPANC-1 showed a benefit for neoadjuvant chemoradiation over upfront surgery in a mixed resectable and borderline population, but NORPACT-1 (2024) found no survival gain from neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX in resectable disease, and the ALLIANCE A021806 trial is testing the question with modern chemotherapy.
claims.note: PREOPANC long-term: benefit across resectable and borderline patients; NORPACT-1 (Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2024): 18-month survival 60% against 73% with no gain; Alliance A021806 (NCT04340141) active, perioperative against adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX.

claims.claim: Adjuvant chemotherapy: Six months of modified FOLFIRINOX for fit patients (PRODIGE 24); gemcitabine plus capecitabine (ESPAC-4) or gemcitabine alone (CONKO-001) for those who cannot tolerate it, started within twelve weeks of surgery.
claims.note: PRODIGE 24 (row ref): six months (24 weeks) of modified FOLFIRINOX, randomised within 3 to 12 weeks of resection (JAMA Oncol 2022); Pancreatic Cancer UK: chemotherapy "should begin in the first 12 weeks after your surgery".

claims.claim: Follow-up: CA 19-9 and CT every three to six months for two years then less often; recurrence is treated as metastatic or locally advanced disease.
claims.note: The row cites only the NCCN guideline, which needs a login. Cancer Research UK's follow-up page describes UK practice differently ("CT scans every 6 months for 5 years") but is not the cited document, so the text is left as it is.

claims.claim: Locally advanced pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is defined by encasement of the superior mesenteric or coeliac artery beyond 180 degrees, an unreconstructable portal or superior mesenteric vein, or aortic involvement, with no metastases on CT.
claims.note: The 180-degree definition is cited to Wikipedia and the NCCN guideline; the NCCN document needs a login and is not on PubMed or PMC. Isaji 2018 (on the parent record) uses the same 180-degree boundary for arterial contact.

claims.claim: Induction chemotherapy is modified FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel for four to six months, extrapolated from the metastatic trials and supported by the NEOLAP and other phase 2 studies.
claims.note: LAP07 (a keyPaper) used 4 months of induction; NEOLAP is a cited phase 2 study. The "four to six months" range rests on the NCCN guideline, which needs a login.

claims.claim: Consolidation chemoradiation after induction did not lengthen survival in LAP07 (2016) but did delay local progression and reduce the need for further chemotherapy, so it remains an option, along with stereotactic body radiotherapy and MR-guided ablative radiotherapy, which deliver high doses to tumours abutting the bowel.
claims.note: LAP07 (JAMA 2016, a keyPaper): no OS difference (15.2 against 16.5 months), "decreased local progression (32% vs 46%". The clause on reduced need for further chemotherapy is not in the abstract and could not be read in full text (JAMA, not open access).

claims.claim: PANOVA-3 (2025) was the first positive phase 3 trial in this stage in a decade: adding tumour treating fields to gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel lengthened survival, and the device was approved in 2026.
claims.note: PANOVA-3 published JCO 2025 with a positive OS result (HR 0.82, p = .039). openFDA device PMA P250034: Optune Pax, decision date 2026-02-11, "intended for treatment of adult patients with locally advanced pancreatic cancer, concomitant with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel". "First positive phase 3 in a decade" was not checked against a source.

claims.claim: NICE NG131 (1.3.8 to 1.3.12) writes one recommendation per Cambridge Prognostic Group: active surveillance is offered first at CPG 1, a choice between all three is offered at CPG 2, radical treatment is offered at CPG 3 with surveillance kept open for men who choose not to be treated immediately, and surveillance is not offered at CPG 4 and 5.
claims.note: NG131 1.3.8 'offer active surveillance' (CPG 1); 1.3.9 'offer a choice between active surveillance, radical prostatectomy or radical radiotherapy' (CPG 2); 1.3.10 offer radical treatment and consider AS for CPG 3; 1.3.11 'Do not offer active surveillance to people with CPG 4 and 5'.

claims.claim: If you were given a risk band instead of a number, the bridge is that CPG 1 is low risk, CPG 2 and 3 are intermediate risk and CPG 4 and 5 are high risk; the group is worked out from your Gleason score or grade group, your PSA and your T stage, and a UK pathology report carries the Gleason score and the grade group together.
claims.note: NG131 rationale: 'The previous intermediate-risk group now consists of some people in CPG 1, and all people in CPG 2 and CPG 3 ... Most people in CPG 4 and CPG 5 align to the previous high-risk group'. The page equated CPG 1 with low risk and CPG 4-5 with high risk outright.
claims.fixed: Bridge restated as NICE gives it: CPG 1 holds the old low-risk group plus some intermediate-risk men; CPG 2-3 the rest of intermediate; most CPG 4-5 men were high risk.

claims.claim: For CPG 1 to 3, NICE (1.3.7) sends the conversation to its box 2, which is a table of what happened to 100 men offered each option in the UK ProtecT trial, and the honest summary of that table is that survival was the same and the harms were not.
claims.note: NG131 1.3.7: 'When discussing treatment options with people with CPG 1, 2 and 3 localised prostate cancer, use box 2'; box 2 uses 'evidence from a large UK trial' framed per 100 patients.

claims.claim: On survival, box 2 reports that at 10 years, 98 out of 100 men offered monitoring, 99 out of 100 offered prostatectomy and 99 out of 100 offered radiotherapy had not died of prostate cancer, and that the evidence does not show a difference between them.
claims.note: Box 2: 'People who had not died of prostate cancer were: 98 out of 100 ... active surveillance 99 out of 100 ... prostatectomy 99 out of 100 ... radiotherapy' at 10 years; 'evidence does not show a difference'.

claims.claim: At a median of 15 years the trial found death from prostate cancer in 17 of 545 men (3.1 percent) on monitoring, 12 of 553 (2.2 percent) after prostatectomy and 16 of 545 (2.9 percent) after radiotherapy, with the overall comparison not significant.
claims.note: Hamdy 2023 abstract: '17 (3.1%) in the active-monitoring group, 12 (2.2%) in the prostatectomy group, and 16 (2.9%) in the radiotherapy group (P = 0.53)'; arms 545/553/545; median follow-up 15 years.

claims.claim: What treatment changed was spread: metastases in 51 men (9.4 percent) on monitoring against 26 (4.7 percent) and 27 (5.0 percent), and clinical progression in 141 (25.9 percent) against 58 (10.5 percent) and 60 (11.0 percent).
claims.note: Hamdy 2023: 'Metastases developed in 51 men (9.4%) ... 26 (4.7%) ... 27 (5.0%)'; 'clinical progression occurred in 141 men (25.9%), 58 (10.5%), and 60 (11.0%)'.

claims.claim: A quarter of the monitoring group, 133 men, were alive at the end of follow-up with no prostate cancer treatment of any kind.
claims.note: Hamdy 2023: 'In the active-monitoring group, 133 men (24.4%) were alive without any prostate cancer treatment at the end of follow-up.'

claims.claim: On continence, box 2 reports moderate to severe incontinence at 6 months in 19 out of 100 men offered prostatectomy against 4 on monitoring and 6 after radiotherapy, and at 6 years in 13, 8 and 5.
claims.note: Box 2: moderate to severe urinary incontinence at 6 months 4/19/6 per 100 (AS/RP/RT); at 6 years 8/13/5.

claims.claim: The trial's own patient-reported figures are blunter: pad use went from 1 percent before treatment to 46 percent at 6 months after surgery, against 4 percent and 5 percent in the other two groups, and was still 17 percent at 6 years and 18 to 24 percent through years 7 to 12.
claims.note: Donovan 2016 (PMC5134995): 'use of absorbent pads increased from 1% at baseline to 46% at 6 months in the prostatectomy group, as compared with 4% ... active-monitoring ... and 5% ... radiotherapy. By year 6, 17%'; Donovan 2023 NEJM Evidence: 'urinary leakage requiring pads occurred in 18 to 24% ... over 7 to 12 years'.

claims.claim: On sexual function, box 2 reports moderate or severe erectile dysfunction at 6 months in 66 out of 100 men offered prostatectomy, 48 after radiotherapy and 29 on monitoring, and at 6 years in 50, 36 and 40.
claims.note: Box 2: moderate or severe ED at 6 months 29/66/48 (AS/RP/RT), at 6 years 40/50/36.

claims.claim: Of the men in the trial, 67 percent could get an erection firm enough for intercourse before anything was done; at 6 months that was 12 percent after surgery, 22 percent after radiotherapy and 52 percent on monitoring, and by year 12 all three groups had converged at a low level.
claims.note: Donovan 2016: 'At baseline, 67% of men reported erections firm enough for intercourse, but by 6 months this rate fell to 52% ... active-monitoring ... 22% ... radiotherapy ... 12% ... prostatectomy'; 2023: 'all converged to low levels of potency by year 12'.

claims.claim: On bowels, radiotherapy is the one that costs: moderate to severe impact of bowel habits on quality of life at 6 months in 10 out of 100 men offered radiotherapy against 3 in each other group, and faecal leakage in 12 percent of the radiotherapy group against 6 percent of the others by year 12.
claims.note: Box 2: moderate to severe impact of bowel habits at 6 months 3/3/10 per 100; Donovan 2023: 'Fecal leakage affected 12% in the radiotherapy group compared with 6% in the other groups by year 12'.

claims.claim: It is what happened to 1,643 UK men aged 50 to 69 with mostly CPG 1 to 3 disease, and the reason to read it is that it names the trade-off rather than gesturing at it.
claims.note: Hamdy 2023: men 50 to 69 years, 1643 enrolled in the UK; NG131 rationale: 'the UK ProtecT trial, which included people with CPG 1 to 3 prostate cancer'.

claims.claim: NICE surrounds the choice with process: a decision aid in the clinic (1.1.6), nomograms with their limits explained (1.1.7), all relevant options discussed even when the local service does not offer them (1.1.9), an assessment by both a specialist surgical oncologist and a specialist clinical oncologist (1.3.5), and an explicit conversation about sexual function, physical appearance, continence and other aspects of masculinity with the man and, if he wishes, his partner (1.1.12).
claims.note: NG131 1.1.6 decision aid; 1.1.7 nomograms; 1.1.9 discuss all options even if not locally available; 1.3.5 specialist surgical oncologist and specialist clinical oncologist; 1.1.12 sexual function, physical appearance, continence, other aspects of masculinity.

claims.claim: On the schedule, NICE NG131 (1.3.19) says to offer hypofractionated radiotherapy, 60 Gy in 20 fractions, using image-guided intensity modulated radiation therapy unless contraindicated, with conventional radiotherapy, 74 Gy in 37 fractions, reserved for people who cannot have the shorter course.
claims.note: NG131 1.3.19: 'offer hypofractionated radiotherapy (60 Gy in 20 fractions) using image-guided IMRT, unless contraindicated or offer conventional radiotherapy (74 Gy in 37 fractions) to people who cannot have hypofractionated radiotherapy'.

claims.claim: On the hormone therapy, NG131 (1.3.21) says to offer radical radiotherapy combined with androgen deprivation therapy rather than either alone for CPG 2, 3, 4 and 5, (1.3.22) six months of it before, during or after the radiotherapy, and (1.3.23) to consider continuing for up to 3 years at CPG 4 and 5 while discussing the benefits and risks of that with the person.
claims.note: NG131 1.3.21 RT+ADT for CPG 2-5; 1.3.22 '6 months of androgen deprivation therapy before, during or after'; 1.3.23 'Consider continuing ... for up to 3 years for people with CPG 4 and 5'.

claims.claim: The radiotherapy's own signature is in the bowel and the bladder in the weeks around treatment, and in the small late risks: NG131 (1.3.6) asks that people are told about the small increase in the risk of colorectal cancer after radical external beam radiotherapy, and (1.3.42) that anyone with signs of radiation-induced enteropathy is cared for by a team with expertise in it.
claims.note: NG131 1.3.6 'small increase in the risk of colorectal cancer after radical external beam radiotherapy'; 1.3.42 team with expertise in radiation-induced enteropathy.

claims.claim: For high-risk disease starting long-term hormone therapy, NG131 (1.3.26) asks for a separate discussion about adding six cycles of docetaxel, with box 3 setting out both sides plainly: clear evidence that progression is delayed by about a year, a five-year survival difference of 84 against 80 out of 100 that might be chance, and 15 out of 100 developing a fever from a low white count with 1 in 100 dying of an infection they might not otherwise have had.
claims.note: NG131 1.3.26 and box 3: 6 appointments 3 weeks apart; progression at about 5 vs 6 years; '80 out of 100 ... compared with 84 out of 100 ... could be because of chance'; '15 out of 100 ... febrile neutropenia'; '1 out of 100 ... died because of infections'.

claims.claim: Hot flushes are the commonest complaint: NICE NG131 (1.4.3) says to offer medroxyprogesterone 20 mg a day for an initial 10 weeks and to evaluate the effect at the end, and (1.4.4) to consider cyproterone acetate 50 mg twice a day for 4 weeks if that fails or is not tolerated; in a randomised trial of 309 men the median daily hot-flush score fell by 83.7 percent on medroxyprogesterone and 94.5 percent on cyproterone at one month, against 47.2 percent on venlafaxine.
claims.note: NG131 1.4.3 medroxyprogesterone 20 mg per day initially for 10 weeks; 1.4.4 cyproterone 50 mg twice a day for 4 weeks. Irani 2010: 309 in efficacy analysis; change at 1 month -47.2% venlafaxine, -94.5% cyproterone, -83.7% medroxyprogesterone.

claims.claim: NG131 (1.4.5) also says plainly that there is no good-quality evidence for complementary therapies here.
claims.note: NG131 1.4.5: 'no good-quality evidence for the use of complementary therapies to treat troublesome hot flushes'.

claims.claim: Bone thinning starts in the first year and increases with time on treatment: in 50,613 men, 19.4 percent of those on androgen deprivation surviving at least five years had a fracture against 12.6 percent of those not on it.
claims.note: Shahinian 2005: 50,613 men; 'Of men surviving at least five years after diagnosis, 19.4 percent of those who received androgen-deprivation therapy had a fracture, as compared with 12.6 percent'.

claims.claim: NICE's four bone sentences run in a specific order: (1.4.12) do not routinely offer bisphosphonates to prevent osteoporosis, (1.4.13) consider assessing fracture risk, (1.4.14) offer bisphosphonates to those who have osteoporosis, and (1.4.15) consider denosumab where bisphosphonates are contraindicated or not tolerated.
claims.note: NG131 1.4.12 do not routinely offer bisphosphonates; 1.4.13 consider assessing fracture risk; 1.4.14 offer bisphosphonates with osteoporosis; 1.4.15 consider denosumab if bisphosphonates contraindicated or not tolerated.

claims.claim: On the heart and the metabolism, in 73,196 Medicare enrollees GnRH agonist use carried adjusted hazard ratios of 1.44 for new diabetes, 1.16 for coronary heart disease, 1.11 for myocardial infarction and 1.16 for sudden cardiac death; in the HERO trial, major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 2.9 percent of 622 men on oral relugolix against 6.2 percent of 308 on leuprolide over 48 weeks.
claims.note: Keating 2006: 73,196 Medicare enrollees; adjusted HR 1.44 diabetes, 1.16 CHD, 1.11 MI, 1.16 sudden cardiac death. HERO: 622 relugolix, 308 leuprolide, 48 weeks, MACE 2.9% vs 6.2%.

claims.claim: NICE NG131 (1.4.18) says to tell people that fatigue is a recognised effect of the therapy and might not be the cancer, and (1.4.19) to offer supervised resistance and aerobic exercise at least twice a week for 12 weeks to reduce fatigue and improve quality of life, which is the single most concrete offer in this section.
claims.note: NG131 1.4.18 fatigue 'might not be because of their prostate cancer'; 1.4.19 'supervised resistance and aerobic exercise at least twice a week for 12 weeks'.

claims.claim: On mood, Prostate Cancer UK says hormone therapy itself can cause tearfulness, mood swings, low mood, anxiety and depression, and a meta-analysis of 18 studies in 168,756 men found a 41 percent higher risk of depression on androgen deprivation.
claims.note: Nead 2017 meta-analysis: 'A meta-analysis of 18 studies among 168,756 individuals found that ADT use conferred a 41% increased risk of depression'. PCUK: hormone therapy 'can make you feel emotional and down ... mood swings, such as getting tearful'.

claims.claim: Gynaecomastia has its own answer: NG131 (1.4.16) says to offer prophylactic radiotherapy to both breast buds within the first month for people starting long-term bicalutamide monotherapy, a single 8 Gy fraction, with weekly tamoxifen considered if that does not work.
claims.note: NG131 1.4.16: bicalutamide monotherapy longer than 6 months, prophylactic radiotherapy to both breast buds within the first month, 'single fraction of 8 Gy'; 1.4.17 'consider weekly tamoxifen'.

claims.claim: And where treatment is long-term and not adjuvant, NG131 (1.4.1) says to consider intermittent therapy, discussing the limited evidence for a reduction in side effects and the effect on progression, with PSA measured every 3 months and treatment restarted at 10 nanogram/ml or above.
claims.note: NG131 1.4.1 consider intermittent therapy (not adjuvant), discuss limited evidence; 1.4.2 'measure PSA every 3 months and restart ... if PSA is 10 nanogram/ml or above'.

claims.claim: In ProtecT, pad use after surgery was 46 percent at six months and 17 percent at six years; radiotherapy barely touched continence at 4 to 5 percent.
claims.note: Donovan 2016: pads 46% at 6 months and 17% at 6 years after prostatectomy; radiotherapy 5% at 6 months, 4% at year 6.

claims.claim: NICE NG131 (1.3.39) requires access to specialist continence services, (1.3.40) referral for consideration of an artificial urinary sphincter for intractable stress incontinence, and (1.3.41) rules out bulking agent injections.
claims.note: NG131 1.3.39 specialist continence services; 1.3.40 artificial urinary sphincter; 1.3.41 'Do not offer injection of bulking agents'.

claims.claim: NICE NG131 (1.3.36) says to offer access to specialist erectile dysfunction services after radical treatment, (1.3.37) to offer PDE5 inhibitor tablets, and (1.3.38) to offer vacuum devices, intraurethral inserts, penile injections or a penile prosthesis where tablets fail or are contraindicated; (1.4.8) extends the same access to men starting hormone therapy and (1.4.10, 1.4.11) repeats the ladder for them.
claims.note: NG131 1.3.36-1.3.38 ED services, PDE5 inhibitors, vacuum devices/intraurethral inserts/injections/prostheses; 1.4.8 access for people starting ADT; 1.4.10-1.4.11 same ladder.

claims.claim: Prostate Cancer UK says to try each type of tablet at least eight times before moving on, that injections work within 5 to 10 minutes and often work even when desire is low, that about 3 in 100 implants get infected and roughly 5 in 100 inflatable implants need replacing within ten years, and that an erection lasting more than four hours is priapism and means going straight to accident and emergency.
claims.note: PCUK: 'Try each type of drug at least eight times'; injections 'within 5 to 10 minutes'; 'Injections should work if you have little or no sexual desire'; 'about 3 in 100 men ... get an infection'; 'around 5 in 100 men ... may need to have it replaced within ten years'; A&E 'if your erection lasts more than four hours'.

claims.claim: Beside all of this NICE NG131 (1.1.13) offers the man and his partner the chance to talk to a healthcare professional experienced in psychosexual issues at any stage, and (1.4.9) considers psychosexual counselling for couples on long-term hormone therapy.
claims.note: NG131 1.1.13 talk to a professional experienced in psychosexual issues at any stage; 1.4.9 consider referral for psychosexual counselling on long-term ADT.

claims.claim: NICE NG131 (1.3.47) says to check it no earlier than 6 weeks after treatment, then at least every 6 months for the first 2 years and at least once a year after that, and (1.3.48) not to do a routine rectal examination while it stays at baseline; (1.3.49) allows remote follow-up after the first 6 months for people with a stable PSA and no significant complications, which for many men means a blood test locally and a phone call.
claims.note: NG131 1.3.47 'no earlier than 6 weeks after treatment, at least every 6 months for the first 2 years, and then at least once a year'; 1.3.48 no routine DRE at baseline PSA; 1.3.49 remote follow-up after at least 6 months.

claims.claim: The most useful sentence in the guideline for anyone watching a number go up is (1.3.55): a rising PSA alone should not mean an immediate change in treatment.
claims.note: NG131 1.3.55: 'biochemical relapse (a rising PSA) alone should not mean an immediate change in treatment is needed'.

claims.claim: What matters is the speed, so (1.3.56) asks for the doubling time to be estimated from at least three measurements over at least six months.
claims.note: NG131 1.3.56: 'Base this on a minimum of 3 measurements over at least a 6-month period.'

claims.claim: After a prostatectomy with no known metastases the standard answer is radiotherapy to the prostate bed (1.3.57), often still given with the aim of cure.
claims.note: NG131 1.3.57: biochemical relapse after radical prostatectomy with no known metastases, 'radical radiotherapy to the prostatic bed'.

claims.claim: Hormone therapy is deliberately held back: (1.3.59) says not to offer it routinely for biochemical relapse unless there is symptomatic local progression, proven metastases, or a doubling time of less than three months, which is the guideline protecting men from years of side effects for a number rather than a disease.
claims.note: NG131 1.3.59: not routinely hormonal therapy for biochemical relapse unless 'symptomatic local disease progression or any proven metastases or a PSA doubling time of less than 3 months'.

claims.claim: Metastatic spinal cord compression happens when deposits in or near the spine press on the spinal cord, and Prostate Cancer UK says about 4 in 100 people with prostate cancer develop it, with the risk highest once the cancer has reached the spine.
claims.note: PCUK MSCC page: 'MSCC isn't common, about 4 in 100 people with prostate cancer develop it', risk if cancer has spread to bones.

claims.claim: NICE NG131 (1.5.19) says to consider zoledronic acid to prevent or reduce skeletal-related events in hormone-relapsed metastatic disease and (1.5.20) bisphosphonates for pain where painkillers and palliative radiotherapy have not been enough; (1.3.35) says not to offer bisphosphonates to prevent bone metastases developing, and (1.4.12) not to offer them routinely to prevent osteoporosis on hormone therapy.
claims.note: NG131 1.5.19 consider zoledronic acid in hormone-relapsed metastatic disease; 1.5.20 bisphosphonates for pain; 1.3.35 'Do not offer bisphosphonates for the prevention of bone metastases'; 1.4.12.

claims.claim: NICE NG131 names trials at several points rather than as a last resort: (1.3.28) says high-intensity focused ultrasound and cryotherapy should be used for localised disease only in controlled trials comparing them with established treatments, which is the answer to give when a focal treatment is offered privately; (1.3.32 and 1.3.33) say the same about immediate post-operative radiotherapy and adjuvant hormone therapy after prostatectomy; (1.3.58) says to consider trial entry for biochemical relapse; and (1.2.5) restricts mapping transperineal template biopsy at initial assessment to trials.
claims.note: NG131 1.3.28 HIFU and cryotherapy only in controlled trials; 1.3.32 and 1.3.33 post-operative RT and adjuvant hormones only in trials; 1.3.58 consider trial entry; 1.2.5 template biopsy only in a trial.

claims.claim: NG131 (1.5.1) asks for tailored information and access to specialist urology and palliative care teams from the point of a metastatic diagnosis, (1.5.2) for palliative interventions to be integrated at any stage into coordinated care with smooth transitions between settings, (1.5.3) for personal preferences and the preferred place of care to be discussed as early as possible with the man, his partner and his carers, and (1.5.5) for a regular assessment of needs rather than waiting to be asked.
claims.note: NG131 1.5.1 tailored information and specialist urology and palliative care; 1.5.2 integrate palliative interventions at any stage; 1.5.3 preferences and preferred place of care as early as possible; 1.5.5 regular assessment of needs.

claims.claim: In the United States, 98.2% of men diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2016-2022 were alive five years later, relative to men of the same age without the disease.
claims.note: SEER Stat Facts prostate: 5-year relative survival 98.2%, SEER 21 2016-2022.

claims.claim: For the 69% found while confined to the prostate and the 14% with regional spread, five-year relative survival is 100%; for the 9% found with distant spread it is 40.1%.
claims.note: SEER: Localized 69% / 100.0%; Regional 14% / 100.0%; Distant 9% / 40.1%.

claims.claim: In the United States, 79.2% of people diagnosed with kidney or renal pelvis cancer in 2016-2022 were alive five years later, relative to people of the same age without the disease.
claims.note: SEER Stat Facts kidney and renal pelvis: 5-year relative survival 79.2%, 2016-2022.

claims.claim: Two thirds (66%) are found while confined to the kidney, often incidentally on a scan for something else, with five-year relative survival of 93.6%; it is 77.6% for regional disease (17% of cases) and 20.3% for distant disease (15% of cases).
claims.note: SEER kidney and renal pelvis: Localized 66% / 93.6%; Regional 17% / 77.6%; Distant 15% / 20.3%.

claims.claim: See a GP if you are having trouble peeing or have other symptoms, if you are over 40 and genetic testing has shown you carry a faulty BRCA2 gene, or if you are worried about your risk; you can ask about a PSA test even without symptoms, and the GP will weigh your risk in deciding whether it is the right test for you (NHS)
claims.note: NHS: 'See a GP if: you're having trouble peeing or have other symptoms ... you're over 40 years old and genetic tests have shown that you have a faulty version of a gene called BRCA2 ... you're worried'; 'You can ask your GP about having a blood test (PSA test) ... even if you do not have symptoms. They'll consider your cancer risk'.

claims.claim: MRI-influenced biopsy is offered at Likert 3 or above; at Likert 1 or 2 omitting biopsy can be considered after a shared discussion of the risks and benefits, and systematic biopsy is offered to anyone who still wants one (NG131 1.2.3, 1.2.4)
claims.note: NG131 1.2.3 'Offer multiparametric MRI-influenced prostate biopsy to people whose Likert score is 3 or more'; 1.2.4 consider omitting biopsy at Likert 1 or 2 after a shared decision, 'If a person opts to have a biopsy, offer systematic prostate biopsy'.

claims.claim: Mapping transperineal template biopsy is not offered as part of an initial assessment outside a trial (NG131 1.2.5)
claims.note: NG131 1.2.5: 'Do not offer mapping transperineal template biopsy as part of an initial assessment, unless as part of a clinical trial.'

claims.claim: After a negative biopsy with an MRI Likert score of 3 or more, the case is discussed at the MDT with a view to repeating the biopsy; after a negative biopsy with Likert 1 or 2, PSA is repeated at 3 to 6 months (NG131 1.2.10, 1.2.12)
claims.note: NG131 1.2.10 Likert 3+ negative biopsy discussed at MDT with a view to repeating biopsy; 1.2.12 Likert 1-2 and negative biopsy, 'repeat PSA at 3 to 6 months'.

claims.claim: CT is considered where MRI is contraindicated and knowing the T or N stage would change management (NG131 1.2.14)
claims.note: NG131 1.2.14: 'Consider CT ... for whom MRI is contraindicated if knowledge of the T or N stage could affect management.'

claims.claim: The pathology report gives the histological type, the Gleason score and the grade group, the tumour length in each core, the percentage of Gleason pattern 4 and whether intraductal or invasive cribriform carcinoma is present; on a prostatectomy specimen it adds extraprostatic extension, seminal vesicle invasion, margins and nodes (RCPath G084, October 2024)
claims.note: RCPath G084 dated October 2024; changes include 'specifying tumour length as a core item', 'requiring percentage Gleason pattern 4 in core biopsies and presence of intraductal carcinoma (IDC)/ invasive cribriform carcinoma'.

claims.claim: Risk band in the UK: the Cambridge Prognostic Groups 1 to 5, which the MDT assigns to every newly diagnosed localised or locally advanced case, combining grade group, PSA and T stage.
claims.note: NG131 1.2.15: 'Urological cancer MDTs should assign a risk category (see table 1) to all people with newly diagnosed localised or locally advanced prostate cancer'; table 1 CPG 1-5 built from Gleason/grade group, PSA and stage.

claims.claim: NICE writes its whole treatment section in these numbers (NG131 1.2.15, table 1)
claims.note: NG131 1.2.15 and table 1; treatment recommendations 1.3.8-1.3.12 are written per CPG.

claims.claim: UK pathology reports stage against UICC TNM 8, which the Royal College of Pathologists dataset names and reprints (G084, October 2024)
claims.note: G084: 'Appendix A TNM (8th edition, UICC)'; 'the dataset has been updated based on UICC TNM8'; dated October 2024.

claims.claim: TNM 9 was published on 3 July 2025 and UICC recommends it from 1 January 2026.
claims.note: UICC announcement (live page returns 406 to scripts; read via Wayback copy of the same page): 'Announcement 03 July 2025 ... UICC recommends that the TNM Classification 9th edition take effect as of 1st of January 2026.'

claims.claim: The prostate T, N and M categories are unchanged; the clinical stage grouping was clarified, and reports are now asked to record the imaging method as a suffix, cT2b(mr) for MRI and N1(PET) for a node found on PSMA PET, because prostate is the malignancy most affected by stage migration (Brierley 2026)
claims.note: Brierley 2026 (PMC13432304): 'Genitourinary classifications are unchanged. 10.1 Prostate Clinical Stage was clarified'; 'carcinoma of the prostate gland is probably the malignancy most affected by stage migration'; 'cT2b (mr) ... N1 (PET), Stage IV (PET)'.

claims.claim: In England 53 percent of prostate cancers with a known stage were diagnosed at stage I or II in 2022, against 37 percent in Scotland in 2023, 57 percent in Northern Ireland and 59 percent in Wales (Cancer Research UK)
claims.note: CRUK: England 53% in 2022; Scotland 37% in 2023; but Northern Ireland 57% is 'On average ... per year between 2015 and 2019' and Wales 59% 'On average ... per year between 2017 and 2019'. The sentence read as if all were recent single years.
claims.fixed: Added the averaging periods for Northern Ireland (2015 to 2019) and Wales (2017 to 2019).

claims.claim: ProtecT randomised 1,643 men with PSA-detected localised disease and found prostate cancer mortality at 15 years of 3.1 percent under monitoring, 2.2 percent after prostatectomy and 2.9 percent after radiotherapy (p=0.53), while 24.4 percent of monitored men were alive at the end of follow-up having never had any treatment.
claims.note: Hamdy 2023: 1643 enrolled; PCSM 3.1%/2.2%/2.9% (P = 0.53); '133 men (24.4%) were alive without any prostate cancer treatment'.

claims.claim: Treatment halves metastasis (9.4 percent monitored against 4.7 and 5.0 percent) but the base rate is low.
claims.note: Hamdy 2023: metastases 9.4% vs 4.7% vs 5.0%.

claims.claim: PIVOT, in a largely PSA-detected United States population, found no significant mortality benefit from surgery over observation at nearly 20 years and more incontinence and erectile dysfunction through 10 years.
claims.note: Wilt 2017: 'After nearly 20 years of follow-up ... surgery was not associated with significantly lower all-cause or prostate-cancer mortality'; 'Urinary incontinence and erectile and sexual dysfunction were each greater with surgery ... through 10 years'.

claims.claim: If radiotherapy is chosen, moderate hypofractionation is standard: CHHiP found 60 Gy in 20 fractions non-inferior to 74 Gy in 37 (5-year freedom from failure 90.6 against 88.3 percent), PROFIT found 60 Gy in 20 non-inferior to 78 Gy in 39 (85 percent in both arms) and RTOG 0415 found 70 Gy in 28 non-inferior to 73.8 Gy in 41 in low-risk disease.
claims.note: CHHiP 2016: 5-year failure-free 88.3% (74 Gy) vs 90.6% (60 Gy), non-inferior. PROFIT: 60 Gy/20 vs 78 Gy/39, '5-year BCF disease-free survival was 85% in both arms'. RTOG 0415: 70 Gy in 28 non-inferior to 73.8 Gy in 41 in low-risk disease.

claims.claim: Five-fraction stereotactic body radiotherapy is non-inferior again (PACE-B, 5-year freedom from failure 95.8 against 94.6 percent) at the price of more late grade 2 or higher genitourinary toxicity (26.9 against 18.3 percent).
claims.note: PACE-B 2024: 5-year freedom from biochemical or clinical failure 95.8% vs 94.6%; late RTOG grade 2+ GU toxicity 26.9% vs 18.3%.

claims.claim: Four to six months of androgen deprivation is added: RTOG 94-08 found 4 months raised 10-year overall survival from 57 to 62 percent, with the benefit confined to intermediate-risk men, and EORTC 22991 found 6 months halved biochemical failure at every radiation dose tested.
claims.note: RTOG 94-08 (Jones 2011): 10-year OS 62% vs 57%, but 'Reanalysis according to risk showed reductions ... primarily among intermediate-risk patients'; 'According to post hoc risk analysis, the benefit was mainly seen in intermediate-risk'. Page said 'confined to'. EORTC 22991: biochemical DFS HR 0.52 with no interaction by dose (correct).
claims.fixed: 'confined to intermediate-risk men' -> 'seen mainly in intermediate-risk men in a post hoc analysis'.

claims.claim: SPCG-7 halved 10-year prostate cancer mortality by adding radiotherapy to hormones (11.9 against 23.9 percent) and the NCIC PR.3/MRC PR07 intergroup trial confirmed it in 1,205 men (overall survival hazard ratio 0.70).
claims.note: SPCG-7: 10-year PCSM 23.9% vs 11.9%, 'halved'. PR.3/PR07 final report: 1,205 patients, OS HR 0.70.

claims.claim: EORTC 22863 showed the reverse addition works too, raising 10-year overall survival from 39.8 to 58.1 percent.
claims.note: Bolla 2010: '10-year overall survival was 39.8% ... radiotherapy alone and 58.1% ... combined treatment'.

claims.claim: Duration is three years, not six months: EORTC 22961 failed to show non-inferiority for 6 months (5-year mortality 19.0 against 15.2 percent, hazard ratio 1.42), RTOG 92-02 found 28 months better than 4 on every endpoint and better for survival in Gleason 8 to 10 disease (45.1 against 31.9 percent at 10 years), and DART 01/05 GICOR found the same even at radiation doses above 76 Gy.
