claims.claim: Melanoma, 2019 data: 12.0 in Jewish and other men against 2.0 in Arab men, and the registry presents its remaining melanoma analyses for Jews and others alone because there are only single Arab cases a year.
claims.note: Melanoma 2019: '12.0 בקרב' Jewish/other men; '2.0 בקרב גברים ערבים'; 'מדי שנה נרשמים מקרים בודדים ... יוצגו שאר נתוני ההיארעות עבור יהודים ואחרים בלבד'

claims.claim: Israel National Cancer Registry, breast cancer in women, 2018 data (September 2021, Hebrew PDF)
claims.note: Citation label: PDF reports 2018 breast data; file name dated September 2021.

claims.claim: Israel National Cancer Registry, colorectal cancer, 2020 data (March 2023, Hebrew PDF)
claims.note: PDF header 'מארס 2023', data to end of 2020.

claims.claim: Israel National Cancer Registry, lung cancer, 2018 data (Hebrew PDF)
claims.note: PDF reports 2018 lung data ('בשנת 2018 אובחנו 2,693 מקרים').

claims.claim: Health Minister's report on smoking in Israel 2025, from the INHIS-5 survey (Hebrew PDF)
claims.note: Title 'דו"ח שר הבריאות על העישון בישראל 2025', with a chapter on INHIS-5.

claims.claim: Israel National Cancer Registry, cutaneous melanoma, 2019 data (May 2022, Hebrew PDF)
claims.note: Melanoma 2019 data; file dated 15052022.

claims.claim: It also finds an enormous amount of the pre-cancer that screening is meant to catch: in 2021, five CIN3 lesions for every invasive cancer, and six times as many per head in Jewish women as in Arab women.
claims.note: 1,648 CIN3 against 304 invasive = 5.4 to 1; CIN3 ASR 43.5 against 7.7 = 5.6 times.

claims.claim: In 2021 the registry recorded 304 invasive cervical cancers, an age-standardised rate of 5.8 per 100,000 in Jewish and other women and 4.3 in Arab women, and 79 deaths.
claims.note: 'בשנת 2021 אובחנו 304 מקרים ... 5.8 ביהודיות ואחרות ו-4.3 בערביות'; 'בשנת 2021 נפטרו 79 נשים'

claims.claim: It ranks Israel 159th of 185 populations for cervical cancer incidence in the Global Cancer Observatory.
claims.note: 'בקרב 185 הרישומים ... ישראל נמצאת במקום ה-159' citing Globocan 2022; the page gave the rank undated.
claims.fixed: Dated as the Global Cancer Observatory's 2022 estimates.

claims.claim: In the same year pre-cancerous lesions were 84.4 percent of all cervical tumour diagnoses: 1,648 CIN3 cases, with age-standardised rates of 43.5 in Jewish and other women against 7.7 in Arab women, and a steep recent rise in Jewish and other women of 14.1 percent a year since 2017.
claims.note: 'כ-84.4% ... 1,648 מקרים ... 43.5 ביהודיות ואחרות ו-7.7 בערביות'; 'עלייה תלולה ומובהקת עד שנת 2021 (APC=14.1%)' after 2017.

claims.claim: Screening is in the basket, and the entitlement has widened: women aged 25 to 54 every three years, where until 2021 it was 30 to 54 and before that 35 to 54, and all four health funds have in practice moved to HPV testing every five years.
claims.note: 'כיום הזכאות היא לנשים בנות 25-54, אחת לשלוש שנים. עד שנת 2021 ... 30-54 וקודם לכן ... 35-54'; 'עברו בפועל ... כל הקופות לשימוש בבדיקת HPV test'; HPV test 'אחת לחמש שנים'.

claims.claim: HPV vaccination has been in the school programme for eighth-graders of both sexes since September 2013.
claims.note: Neither cited source (registry PDF, MoH parent sheet) gives a start date or the sexes. A peer-reviewed source states: 'the quadrivalent HPV vaccine was introduced in 2013 into the national immunization program for eighth-grade girls, later extended to boys'. 'Both sexes since September 2013' is wrong.
claims.fixed: Now reads: entered the school programme for eighth-grade girls in 2013 and was later extended to boys. Added Chodick and Strassberg (J Clin Med 2026) as a link.

claims.claim: Two participation series exist and should not be merged: the registry, citing the national quality indicators programme for 2023, gives 68.7 percent of women aged 25 to 54 screened in the previous three years, while the programme's own 2024 publication gives 66.7 percent for the same age band on a definition that now admits five-yearly HPV testing and self-testing.
claims.note: Registry: '68.7% בשנת 2023' (25-54, previous 3 years) correct; 2024 deck: 'שיעור ארצי (2024): 66.7%' for screening 'בתדירות המומלצת'. The deck does not say the definition admits five-yearly HPV testing and self-testing. The cited PDF URL now 404s; the same deck, dated 18.5.2026, is at the -1.pptx URL.
claims.fixed: Unsupported definition clause replaced with 'screened at the recommended frequency'; NPQICH link repointed from the dead PDF to the live deck.

claims.claim: Mean age at death in 2021 was 63.3 in Jewish and other women and 45.6 in Arab women, on small numbers the registry itself flags.
claims.note: 'הגיל הממוצע ... 63.3 ... בנשים יהודיות ואחרות, ו-45.6 ... בנשים ערביות'; small Arab numbers flagged ('מבוססים על מספרים קטנים מאוד').

claims.claim: Israel National Cancer Registry, cervical cancer, 2021 data (January 2025, Hebrew PDF)
claims.note: PDF header 'עדכון נתוני היארעות ותמותה, ינואר 2025', 2021 data.

claims.claim: Mammography every two years for average-risk women aged 50 to 74 began nationally in 1995, after an Israel Cancer Association awareness campaign from 1990; annual faecal occult blood testing from 50 to 74 began in 2005 on the same initiative.
claims.note: The figures are right, but the 1990 campaign and 1995 national mammography start appear only in the breast registry PDF, which this card did not cite: 'בשנת 1990 החל מסע פרסום של האגודה למלחמה בסרטן ... ובשנת 1995 הושקה התכנית הלאומית'. FOBT 2005 is in the cited CRC PDF: 'הופעלה בשנת 2005 תכנית לאומית ... ביוזמת האגודה למלחמה בסרטן'.
claims.fixed: Added the breast registry PDF to the card's links.

claims.claim: In the 2024 quality indicators data, 72.3 percent of women aged 50 to 74 had had a mammogram, 73.8 percent in the general population, 68.6 percent in Arab society and 60.0 percent among the ultra-Orthodox, with 76.8 percent in the top socioeconomic deciles against 65.5 percent in the bottom.
claims.note: Deck chart values 2024: national 72.3%; general 0.7376, Arab 0.6859, ultra-Orthodox 0.5998; deciles 9+10 0.768, 1+2 0.655.

claims.claim: Bowel screening reached 65.0 percent nationally, 65.9, 64.1 and 53.7 percent by the same three groups.
claims.note: Bowel 2024: national 65.0%; general 0.6593, Arab 0.6406, ultra-Orthodox 0.5368.

claims.claim: Cervical screening at the recommended frequency reached 66.7 percent of women aged 25 to 54, with the largest social gap of the four indicators: 82.6 percent in the top deciles against 46.0 percent in the bottom.
claims.note: Cervical 2024: national 66.7%; deciles 9+10 0.8257, 1+2 0.4604. That 36.5-point gap is the largest of the four indicators (mammography 11.3, bowel 9.6, colonoscopy 25.8).

claims.claim: The indicator that most affects whether screening saves a life is the follow-up: only 65.5 percent of people with a positive faecal occult blood test had a colonoscopy within 180 days, 75.9 percent in the top deciles against 50.1 percent in the bottom, a 25.8 point gap.
claims.note: Colonoscopy after positive FOBT 2024: national 65.5%; deciles 9+10 0.759, 1+2 0.501 (gap 25.8).

claims.claim: The programme's own summary of the 2024 data is that screening rose and gaps narrowed.
claims.note: Summary slides: 'עליה בביצוע ממוגרפיה בחברה הערבית ...', '... וצמצום הפערים', 'שנת 2024 כבר הדגימה צמצום פערים, למרות המלחמה'.

claims.claim: The outcome the bowel programme was built for is visible in the registry: 37 percent of new colorectal patients in 2020 were diagnosed at in-situ or stage 1, double the 19.9 percent of 2000, and the share metastatic at diagnosis fell from 14.6 to 8.2 percent.
claims.note: '37% מהחולים החדשים בשנת 2020 אובחנו בשלב מחלה מוקדם. שיעור זה כפול ... (19.9%) 2000'; metastatic 'מ-14.6% בשנת 2000 ל-8.2% בשנת 2020' (among cases with stage information).

claims.claim: Israel Cancer Association, annual report 2025 (English PDF)
claims.note: ICA annual report, 'Fiscal Year 2025', English.

claims.claim: Israel National Cancer Registry, colorectal cancer, 2020 data (Hebrew PDF)
claims.note: Colorectal 2020 data PDF.

claims.claim: Written into the 2021 report, in the registry's own words: the Global Cancer Observatory figures are estimated, not measured, and the data for Israel there do not separate Arabs from Jews and others, and therefore the rates on that site cannot be compared with the true rates the registry measures.
claims.note: 'הנתונים באתר מעודכנים לשנת 2022 אולם הם נתונים מוערכים, לא מדודים ... לא מפרידים בין ערבים ויהודים/אחרים, ומשום כך לא ניתן להשוות את השיעורים ... עם השיעורים האמתיים שמודד הרישום' (not presented as a verbatim quotation).

claims.claim: Stage has been recorded since 2000 but only insofar as the information reaches the registry, and cannot be assigned when there was no surgery, when treatment preceded the first pathology, or when the report came from a death notification; published completeness runs from about 86 percent for cervix and 79 percent for melanoma to about 72 percent for breast and 56 to 77 percent for colorectum.
claims.note: The figures are correct but come from site reports this card did not cite: cervical 'לכ-86% המקרים'; melanoma 'קיימים עבור 79%'; breast 'עבור כ-72%'; CRC 'עבור 77%-56%', with stage registration 'החל ... בשנת 2000' and no stage for death notices, neoadjuvant treatment or no surgery.
claims.fixed: Added the breast, colorectal, cervical and melanoma registry PDFs to the card's links.

claims.claim: The registry's reportable set is tumour registration, not treatment: it records tumour characteristics, and since 2016 oestrogen, progesterone and HER2 status for invasive breast cancer, complete for 67 percent of 2018 diagnoses, but no evidence was found that it records treatment given.
claims.note: Breast PDF (not cited on this card): 'הוחל באיסוף ... ER ... PR ... HER2 ... משנת 2016'; 'בשנת 2018, פרטים מלאים ... נרשמו עבור 67%'.
claims.fixed: Breast registry PDF added to the card's links.

claims.claim: The most recent general incidence and mortality update covers diagnosis year 2021 and was published in August 2024, a lag of about two years and eight months, and the registry warns that a year's first publication is provisional: its 2020 report reflected only about 92 percent of expected cases.
claims.note: August 2024 publication of the 2021 data is correct (PDF header 'אוגוסט 2024'), and basal/squamous skin carcinomas are excluded per Moore 2021 ('excluding basal and squamous cell carcinomas of the skin'). The 'about 92 percent of expected cases' for the 2020 report is in neither the 2021 report nor Moore; the 2020 report PDF could not be retrieved.
claims.fixed: Removed the unsourced clause about the 2020 report reflecting 92 percent of expected cases.

claims.claim: The National Health Insurance Law of 1994 entitles every resident to a defined basket.
claims.note: Knesset RIC: 'חוק ביטוח בריאות ממלכתי, התשנ"ד-1994 מעגן את זכאותו של כל תושב ישראל לסל שירותי הבריאות המוגדר בחוק'

claims.claim: What the law does is make the basket zero-sum, because section 8(e) forbids adding a service without finding the money for it.
claims.note: Law s.8(e): 'לא ייווסף שירות לסל שירותי הבריאות ללא תשלום ... אלא אם כן נמצא לכך מקור מימון נוסף'

claims.claim: So since 1998 the Health and Finance Ministers have appointed a public committee each year, and the procedure has been written down since February 2010, after the Israel Medical Association took the state to the High Court over the absence of published rules.
claims.note: 1998 start and the February 2010 procedure are sourced (Comptroller: 'נוהל עדכון סל שירותי הבריאות - פברואר 2010'). Nothing on the card (law, Knesset RIC, IJTAHC, ESMO Open) says the Israel Medical Association went to the High Court; the IMA position paper read here doesn't say so either.
claims.fixed: Removed the unsourced High Court clause.

claims.claim: The 2022 committee had four doctors, four economists, four health fund representatives, four public representatives, a chair and a coordinator.
claims.note: Knesset RIC: 'בשנת 2022 כללה ועדה זו ארבעה רופאים, ארבעה כלכלנים, ארבעה נציגי קופות החולים, ארבעה נציגי ציבור, יו"ר ומרכזת' (18, as the title says).

claims.claim: The number that decides everything: 650 million shekels against a basket of about 75 billion
claims.note: 650m for 2026 (ynet); NII Table 9: 2024 basket cost estimate 75,474 million.

claims.claim: It has never once been that, and in 21 of 24 years it was below even the lower threshold they proposed.
claims.note: Comptroller: 'ב-21 (כ-90%) מ-24 השנים ... שיעור התוספת היה קטן מ-1.5%, הרף התחתון עליו המליצו הוועדות'; IJTAHC: allocation 'varies between 0.8 and 1.7 percent', so never 2%.

claims.claim: It was 150 million shekels in 1998, 300 million a year from 2011 to 2013, 500 million from 2017 to 2021, 550 million in 2022 and 650 million in each of 2023, 2025 and 2026; the State Comptroller's own table gives 460 million for 2017 to 2019 where its headline text says 500 million, a discrepancy inside one report that is not resolved here.
claims.note: 150m 1998 and 500m 2017-2021 match the Comptroller and the Knesset RIC. 300m 2011-2013 is in the IMA paper ('יעמוד תקציב עדכון הסל בשנים 2011-2013 על 300 מיליון'), and 550m 2022 is in the Adva Center paper ('תוספת קלה שניתנה בשנת 2022 והגיעה ל-550 מיליון'); both papers were cited elsewhere on the page but not on this card. 650m 2023 (Knesset/IJTAHC), 2025 (Calcalist), 2026 (ynet). The Comptroller's 460m in Table 1 is explained by its own footnote 13, 'לא כולל סכום שהוקצה לרפואת שיניים', so it is not an unexplained discrepancy. (ynet, 29 Dec 2020, reports a 550m agreement for 2021 against the Comptroller's and Knesset's 500m; noted, not changed.)
claims.fixed: Now explains that the 460m table leaves out dental care, per its footnote; added the Adva Center and IMA papers to the card's links for the 550m and 300m figures.

claims.claim: For 2026 the government's decision had been 550 million and the Ministry held the frame at 650 million, buying 107 technologies for 86,450 patients.
claims.note: ynet 19 Feb 2026, the minister: 'הוכנסו 107 טכנולוגיות חדשות לטובת 86,450 מטופלים ... מסגרת סל גבוהה מאשר החלטת הממשלה, שהייתה 550 מיליון'

claims.claim: Against it, the cost of the basket the funds are responsible for was 56,729 million shekels in 2020 and an estimated 75,474 million in 2024.
claims.note: NII Annual Report 2024 Table 9: 56,729 (2020) and 75,474 (2024, 'על פי אומדן').

claims.claim: The Tal Committee of 1999 recommended anchoring a technology coefficient of 2 percent of basket cost in law; the German Committee of 2014 proposed a floor of 0.8 percent; the Ministry itself recommended 1.5 to 2 percent in 2019.
claims.note: Comptroller: Tal 1999 '2% מעלות סל'; German 2014 'לא תפחת מ-0.8%'; Ministry January 2019 'בין 1.5% ל-2%'.

claims.claim: The State Comptroller's finding, read from its own report, is that in 21 of the 24 years from 1998 to 2021, about 90 percent of them, the supplement was below 1.5 percent of basket cost, and in four of them, about 15 percent, below 0.8 percent.
claims.note: 'ב-21 (כ-90%) מ-24 השנים שבתקופה 1998 ועד 2021 ... קטן מ-1.5% ... בארבע (כ-15%) ... קטן מ-0.8%'

claims.claim: The Ministry's own published figure is that the allocation varies between 0.8 and 1.7 percent and has stabilised around 0.9 percent.
claims.note: IJTAHC (MoH authors): 'varies between 0.8 and 1.7 percent of the entire health service basket and has stabilized in recent years around 0.9 percent'

claims.claim: The Taub Center calculates that had the basket been updated since 1995 on the indices the professional committees recommended it would stand at 85 to 96 billion shekels rather than the 56.7 billion of 2020, a cumulative shortfall of about 26 percent, and argues the erosion is what built Israel's private health market.
claims.note: Taub: 85-96 billion against 56.7 billion is right, but the 26% is a separate calculation: 'according to the demographic coefficient and the healthcare price coefficient ... the basket's cumulative deficit is currently about 26%'. The sentence presented it as the gap between the 85-96 and 56.7 figures (which would be about a third).
claims.fixed: Now says the 26 percent is the shortfall on population growth and health prices alone.

claims.claim: Demand is not the constraint: the Ministry estimates that drugs and technologies worth about 2 billion shekels a year reach the committee's final decision phase having already been judged to meet a clear medical need.
claims.note: Comptroller, Ministry response: 'מדי שנה מגיעות לישורת האחרונה ... תרופות וטכנולוגיות בעלות כוללת של כשני מיליארד ש"ח ... ונמצא כי יש בהן צורך רפואי ברור'

claims.claim: Across a quarter of a century cancer has taken more of the annual budget than any other field, about 38 percent on average.
claims.note: IJTAHC: 'Oncology ... comprised the largest number and proportion of approved technologies throughout 1998-2023 (mean 38 percent)', in a figure of budget share by domain.

claims.claim: But the yearly figure is volatile: 19 percent in 2025, when an infant vaccine outbid it, and 52 percent in 2026.
claims.note: 19% (124 of 650m) in 2025 and 52% in 2026 are correct, but the infant RSV vaccine (109m) did not by itself outbid oncology (124m). The infectious-disease category (160m) did: Calcalist '160 מיליון שקל הוקצו למחלות זיהומיות לעומת 124 מיליון לאונקולוגיה'.
claims.fixed: Now reads 'when infectious disease, led by an infant vaccine, outbid it'.

claims.claim: The Ministry of Health's own published account of its committee states that from 1998 to 2023 oncology, including haemato-oncology, comprised the largest number and proportion of approved technologies, a mean of 38 percent, ahead of cardiovascular at 10 percent, neurology at 7 percent and endocrinology at 6 percent.
claims.note: IJTAHC: 'largest number and proportion ... 1998-2023 (mean 38 percent), followed by cardiovascular (10 percent), neurology (7 percent), and endocrinology (mainly diabetes 6 percent)'

claims.claim: The State Comptroller puts the oncology drug budget at 37 percent of the average annual supplement across 2016 to 2021.
claims.note: Comptroller: 'התקציב למימון התרופות האונקולוגיות שיעורו 37% מסך התוספת התקציבית הממוצעת לסל בשנים 2021-2016'

claims.claim: About half the 2019 budget went to cancer.
claims.note: No source on the card (IJTAHC, Comptroller, ESMO Open, Calcalist, ynet) gives a 2019 oncology share. ESMO Open says only 'In most recent years ∼30% of the budget expansion was allocated to oncology new drugs'.
claims.fixed: Removed the sentence 'About half the 2019 budget went to cancer.'

claims.claim: In 2021 it was 8 percent, which the Israeli authors attribute to pandemic priorities and a large diabetes allocation.
claims.note: ESMO Open: 'this was smaller in 2021 (8%), due to COVID-19 considerations and also a significant allocation for the treatment of diabetes'

claims.claim: In 2025, 124 million shekels of 650 million, about 19 percent, went to oncology, beaten for the first time by infectious disease at about 160 million, of which an infant respiratory syncytial virus vaccine alone took 109 million.
claims.note: Calcalist: 124m oncology, 160m infectious disease, RSV vaccine 109m are correct. 'For the first time' is not in the source, which says only that the committee prioritised infectious over oncological diseases 'שבדרך כלל מקבלות את רוב המשאבים'.
claims.fixed: Removed 'for the first time'.

claims.claim: In 2026 oncology and haemato-oncology took 52 percent, about 340 million shekels, while infectious disease fell from 24 percent to 1 percent.
claims.note: ynet: 'מהווה 52% מהסל בסכום של כ-340 מיליון שקל'; 'בשנה שעברה היווה תחום המחלות הזיהומיות 24% מהסל, אך השנה צומצם ל-1% בלבד'

claims.claim: The other pressure is price: the Ministry reports that the average yearly cost of an oncology drug approved by the committee rose, inflation-adjusted, from about 60,000 shekels per patient in 2009 to over 130,000 in 2018, which it converts in the same sentence to about 18,000 and 43,000 US dollars.
claims.note: IJTAHC: 'from an average yearly cost of approximately 60,000 NIS ($18,000) per patient per new drug in 2009 to over 130,000 NIS ($43,000) in 2018 (figures adjusted for inflation)'

claims.claim: Calcalist on the 2025 basket (6 February 2025, Hebrew, archived)
claims.note: Calcalist byline '17:00, 06.02.25'; archived copy readable.

claims.claim: The routes out, as the State Comptroller enumerates them, are the health fund's exceptions committee, private or commercial insurance, a clinical trial, compassionate supply from the manufacturer, the National Health Insurance Ombudsman, the labour court, personal or pharmacy import, and, rarely, treatment abroad under section 11.
claims.note: The Comptroller lists the exceptions committee, private insurance, a research group, compassionate supply, the ombudsman ('נציבות הקבילות') and the labour court. Personal or pharmacy import is not in its list or on any card source. Treatment abroad is section 11 of the law ('בהתקיים נסיבות רפואיות מיוחדות'), not a Comptroller route.
claims.fixed: Removed personal or pharmacy import; treatment abroad now attributed to section 11 of the law in special medical circumstances.

claims.claim: About 6,000 requests reached the four funds' exceptions committees in total over 2014 to 2017, roughly doubling across those years, with 60 to 65 percent approved, at a cost the funds put at about 200 million shekels a year.
claims.note: 'בשנים 2017-2014 הוגשו לוועדות החריגים ... כ-6,000 בקשות (בסכום של כ-200 מיליון ש"ח בשנה לפי הערכת הקופות) ... ואף כמעט הוכפל; שיעור הבקשות שאושרו ... 60% עד 65%'

claims.claim: And an Israeli study of compassionate use counted 3,284 treatments between 2020 and 2024 using 596 distinct products across 1,361 conditions, 63 percent of them continuations of a study drug, the commonest being belantamab mafodotin at 9 percent and trametinib at 8.6 percent;
claims.note: Schwartzberg 2025: '3,284 compassionate treatments ... 596 distinct medicinal products to address 1,361 conditions'; 'continuation of study drug in 63%'; 'Belantamab mafodotin and Trametinib ... 9% and 8.6%'

claims.claim: 77 percent were given in large central hospitals and 49 percent in the Central district, with the Southern district lowest; and 60 percent of the commonest technologies, 13 of 22, later entered the basket, typically after more than two years of compassionate use.
claims.note: 'large central hospitals (77%) and the central district (49%), with the southern district showing the least usage'; '60% of the most common technologies (13 out of 22) were subsequently included ... compassionate use that exceeded two years'

claims.claim: The widespread belief that Israel's supplementary plans cover off-basket cancer drugs is wrong: section 10(b)(4) of the law states that a supplementary plan shall not include life-saving or life-extending medicines, and those drugs were removed from the plans in three tranches up to 2010 in exchange for basket additions.
claims.note: Law s.10(b)(4): 'התכנית לא תכלול תרופות מצילות חיים או מאריכות חיים'; IMA paper: 'הוקצו בתמורה להוצאתן של תרופות וטכנולוגיות מאריכות חיים ... בשלוש פעימות עד לשנת 2010'

claims.claim: That is the job of commercial insurance, which the Central Bureau of Statistics Social Survey of 2017 found 22 percent of the population held.
claims.note: Comptroller fn 104: 'מתוך הסקר החברתי 2017 עולה כי ל-22% מהאוכלוסייה יש ביטוח לתרופות שאינן כלולות בסל'

claims.claim: What being left out costs is visible in the 2026 round: lecanemab for early Alzheimer's disease reached the final stage and was excluded at about 160,000 shekels per patient a year after a price reduction, and the ynet report notes those patients will go on paying from their own pockets or through private insurance.
claims.note: ynet: 'לקמבי, שהגיעה לדיונים הסופיים, עמדה על כ-160 אלף שקלים לחולה לשנה לאחר הורדת מחיר'; caption 'החולים ימשיכו לשלם מכיסם או על חשבון הביטוח הפרטי'

claims.claim: Schwartzberg et al., Compassionate use in Israel 2020-2024 (Isr J Health Policy Res 2025)
claims.note: DOI 10.1186/s13584-025-00730-3, 'Trends in compassionate use of medicinal products: Israel 2020-2024', Schwartzberg E et al.

claims.claim: The State Comptroller's May 2022 report is the sharpest published critique and was read here in the original.
claims.note: Report dated 'אייר התשפ"ב | מאי 2022'.

claims.claim: Contrary to the 2010 procedure, which requires an economic evaluation to accompany an application, economic evaluations are almost never submitted: in the three years 2018 to 2020 the technology assessment division received one, and told the auditors it is not functionally equipped to carry out economic evaluations, in staff, tools or methods.
claims.note: 'בשנים 2020-2018 הוגשה הערכה כלכלית אחת. האגף ציין ... כי הוא אינו ערוך מהבחינה הפונקציונלית לביצוע הערכות כלכליות, הן מבחינת היקף כוח האדם ... והן מבחינת הכלים והמתודולוגיות'

claims.claim: The Ministry's technology forum, all of whose members are Ministry staff, rejected 46 percent of non-drug and 9 percent of drug requests over 2018 to 2021 without those rejections or their reasons reaching the committee or the applicant.
claims.note: 'כל חברי הפורום הם נציגי משרד הבריאות'; 46% and 9% correct; 'הפרטים בנוגע לדחיות אינם מובאים לידיעת ועדת הסל'. The report says the procedure requires the forum to notify the applicant ('עליו לשלוח הודעה למגיש הבקשה'), so 'or the applicant' is not supported. The plain summary's 'never tells rejected applicants why' was wrong for the same reason.
claims.fixed: Detail now says the details of rejections do not reach the committee; plain summary changed to 'does not tell the committee what a Ministry forum screened out'.

claims.claim: The sub-committee that prices submissions has no public representative, admits no journalists where the main committee does, and publishes no protocols; the main committee's protocols were published 109 to 160 working days late over 2018 to 2020.
claims.note: Sub-committee: 'לא משתתף בה נציג ציבור, גם עיתונאים אינם מורשים לנכוח ... הפרוטוקולים ... אינם מתפרסמים'; protocols 'עיכוב של בין 109 ל-160 ימי עבודה' in 2018-2020.

claims.claim: Costings rest on disease registries with no power to compel reporting, and the Comptroller singles out the National Cancer Registry for holding little information on disease stage, which matters because cancer drugs were up to 37 percent of the addition over 2016 to 2021.
claims.note: The report says most registries run under the Patient's Rights Law with 'אין חובה למסירת הנתונים', but the cancer registry has mandatory reporting under the 1982 regulations ('חלה על בתי חולים ... חובת מסירת נתונים'). Stage finding and 'עד כדי 37%' are correct.
claims.fixed: Now says 'disease registries, most of them with no power to compel reporting'.

claims.claim: Ten technologies took 62 percent of the whole addition over those years, 1.7 billion of about 2.7 billion shekels, with the remaining 40 percent spread across about a hundred;
claims.note: 'הן מהוות 62% מעלות התוספת כולה המסתכמת בכ-1.7 מיליארד ש"ח מתוך כ-2.7' is correct. The 40% is a per-year figure from another passage ('למעט שנת 2020, בכל אחת משנים 2021-2016 כ-60% ... יתרת הנתח - כ-40% - ... כ-100'). Set beside the 62% period total, it did not add up.
claims.fixed: Now says that in every year but 2020 about 40 percent was left for the hundred or so others.

claims.claim: 31 percent of technologies added in 2016 to 2021 came at no cost.
claims.note: Summary: '31% חלקן הכמותי של התרופות והטכנולוגיות ללא עלות שהוכללו בסל בשנים 2021-2016'

claims.claim: Israeli oncologists are not uniformly comfortable either: in a survey of 127 of them, 59 percent said they often face dilemmas about recommending unfunded treatments to patients in financial difficulty without private insurance, and 38 percent feel uncomfortable discussing cost with patients.
claims.note: Bashkin et al. abstract: 'surveyed 127 oncologists ... 59% indicated that they often face dilemmas ... Over a third (38%) stated that they felt uncomfortable discussing the cost'

claims.claim: Recommending unfunded innovative cancer therapies: ethical versus clinical perspectives among oncologists (Curr Oncol 2021)
claims.note: Curr Oncol 2021, Bashkin O et al., title matches.

claims.claim: Shmueli, Do the equity-efficiency preferences of the Israeli Basket Committee match those of Israeli health policy makers? (Isr J Health Policy Res 2017)
claims.note: Shmueli A, Isr J Health Policy Res 2017, title matches.

claims.claim: Three conflicts in the sources are reported rather than reconciled: whether the one year with no basket supplement was 2003 or 2004; the State Comptroller's own report giving 460 million shekels in a table where its headline text says 500 million for 2017 to 2019; and the registry's own 2021 report giving Jewish and other women's mortality rate as 66.7 in one paragraph and 64.7 in another, and a 2021 prevalence total of 98,813 against components summing to 96,813.
claims.note: 2003 vs 2004 is a real conflict (Knesset RIC 'מלבד שנת 2003'; IJTAHC 'Missing data in 2004, the single year ... when no budget was allocated'). 66.7/64.7 and 98,813 against 43,311+53,502=96,813 are real. But the Comptroller's 460 against 500 is explained by its own footnote 13 (excludes dental care), so it is not a conflict.
claims.fixed: Dropped the 460/500 item; now 'Two conflicts'.

claims.claim: At November 2025 the National Insurance Institute's register counted 9,796,872 residents insured under the law: Clalit 4,954,452 (50.6 percent), Maccabi 2,710,338 (27.7 percent), Meuhedet 1,391,017 (14.2 percent) and Leumit 741,065 (7.6 percent).
Clalit's share has drifted down from 52.3 percent in 2015 while Maccabi rose from 25.2 percent; the same publication gives Leumit as 7.5 percent in its abstract and 7.6 percent in its tables.
claims.note: '52.3% בשנת 2015 ל-50.6% בשנת 2025'; Maccabi 'מ-25.2%'; abstract gives Leumit 'ו-7.5% בקופת חולים לאומית', tables 7.6.

claims.claim: Of the cost of the basket the funds are responsible for, the Institute's own table puts health insurance contributions at 44.5 percent in 2024 and the state budget at 49.0 percent, with the funds' own income from members fixed at 6.45 percent, a share legislated in 2008 and raised from the 5.4 percent that applied until 2007.
claims.note: NII Annual Report 2024 Table 9: 2024 health insurance contributions 44.5, state budget 49.0, own income 6.45; footnote: 'בחוק התוכנית לסיוע כלכלי ל-2008 נקבע ... 6.45% מעלות הסל (במקום 5.4% עד 2007)'.

claims.claim: The contribution itself is 3.23 percent of income on the lower band and 5.17 percent above it in 2026, with a minimum of 123 shekels a month.
claims.note: NII chapter 4: 'הועלה שיעור דמי ביטוח בריאות ממלכתי משנת 2025 – במדרגה המלאה ... ל-5.165% ... ובמדרגה המופחתת ל-3.235%'. The cited 2024 report cannot vouch for '2026', and the minimum of 123 shekels a month is not in it (it gives a general NII minimum of 116 shekels in 2024).
claims.fixed: Now reads 3.235 and 5.165 percent 'since 2025'; removed the unsourced 123-shekel minimum.

claims.claim: Clalit holds about 55 percent of all insured aged 65 and over and 66.3 percent of residents of the periphery against 48.0 percent elsewhere, which is the same point from the other side.
claims.note: 'חלקה בקבוצת גיל זו ... כ-55%'; 'בסוף 2025 66.3% מתושבי הפריפריה היו מבוטחים בכללית לעומת 48% מהתושבים שלא בפריפריה'.

claims.claim: Maccabi's entitlements page states that such patients are exempt from the quarterly co-payment and from co-payment on basket medicines designated for the disease, with a ceiling on other basket medicines and consumables that its own two documents give as 367 shekels a month in the January 2026 tariff and 379 on the April severe-illness page; both are reported here.
claims.note: Maccabi entitlements page (updated 01.4.26): exemption from quarterly co-payment and disease medicines; 'תקרת השתתפות העצמית בתרופות מסל הבריאות שאינן ייעודיות למחלה, כולל בציוד מתכלה, היא 379 ₪ לחודש'. Maccabi's current tariff (October 2026) also gives 379. The 367 'January 2026 tariff' is superseded and was not linked.
claims.fixed: Ceiling now given as 379 shekels a month; dropped the superseded 367; added Maccabi's October 2026 tariff PDF as a link.

claims.claim: Leumit's published schedule, current at 1 July 2026, exempts severe illness patients from co-payment for outpatient clinic and institute visits and from co-payment on their disease medicines.
claims.note: Leumit 'מעודכנים נכון ל- 01 ביולי, 2026': 'חולים במחלה קשה* פטור מהשתתפות בביקור במרפאות חוץ או במכונים; פטור מהשתתפות עצמית בעד תרופות הייעודיות עבור מחלתם'.

claims.claim: The figures differ by fund by more than a little and no single national figure should be quoted: a specialist visit is 33 shekels a quarter at Maccabi and 41 at Leumit; the family quarterly ceiling is 257 against 313.40; the accident and emergency charge, where no exemption applies, is 1,199 at Maccabi and a flat 600 at Leumit.
claims.note: Leumit side correct (specialist 41, family ceiling 313.40, A&E 600). Maccabi's current tariff, 'מעודכן - אוקטובר 2026', gives specialist '₪ 34 לרבעון לכל רופא', family ceiling '₪ 266 לרבעון', A&E '₪ 1,259 נכון ל-1 באוקטובר 2026', against the page's 33, 257 and 1,199. Those Maccabi figures were also on no linked page.
claims.fixed: Maccabi figures updated to 34, 266 and 1,259 (from October 2026); tariff PDF linked.

claims.claim: Transport is confirmed at both: a taxi at the full one-way fare or half of both ways, an ambulance to the Magen David Adom tariff with a doctor's approval, a private car at a litre of fuel per 10 kilometres each way, and public transport in full.
claims.note: Correct, but Maccabi's transport terms were not on the linked Maccabi page. Maccabi tariff: 'במונית: החזר של 100% לכיוון אחד או 50% ל-2 הכיוונים'; ambulance up to the MDA tariff 'מותנה באישור רופא מטפל'; 'ליטר דלק לכל 10 ק"מ'; public transport 'החזר עלות מלאה'. Leumit: public transport no charge, taxi/ambulance with prior fund approval at 50% participation, '1 ליטר דלק' per 10 km.
claims.fixed: Added Maccabi's tariff PDF to the card's links.

claims.claim: Leumit: basket co-payment schedule (Hebrew, current at 1 July 2026)
claims.note: Page header 'מעודכנים נכון ל- 01 ביולי, 2026'.

claims.claim: Section 10 of the National Health Insurance Law sets conditions that make these plans unlike private insurance elsewhere: the fund must accept any applicant regardless of health or means, the price must be uniform within each age band, the plan must be self-financing, and it pays for services rather than cash, except for nursing and choice of operating surgeon.
claims.note: Law s.10(c)(1) accept regardless of health or means; 10(e) 'מחיר התכנית יהיה אחיד לכל קבוצת גיל'; 10(f) expenses not to exceed income; 10(b)(3) services in kind 'למעט שירותי סיעוד ולמעט בחירת רופא מנתח'.

claims.claim: Section 10(b)(4) then forbids the plan from including life-saving or life-extending medicines.
claims.note: '(4) התכנית לא תכלול תרופות מצילות חיים או מאריכות חיים'.

claims.claim: The common framing that supplementary plans cover off-basket drugs up to a monetary ceiling does not survive reading a rulebook: Leumit's, current at July 2026, handles off-basket medicines as a named-drug discount list of more than 600 medicines with per-drug indications and co-payment percentages, not an open ceiling; ceilings belong to commercial policies.
claims.note: Leumit Gold/Silver: 'הנחות על חיסונים ותרופות - על למעלה מ-600 תרופות שאינן בסל!'; rulebook July 2026 (חוברת ... 0726).

claims.claim: What supplementary cover verifiably adds for a cancer patient is surgery in a private hospital or a public hospital's private service with choice of surgeon, a second opinion including on a pathology report, treatment abroad, genetic testing for colorectal, breast and ovarian predisposition, and a wig up to 1,866 shekels on the higher Leumit tier.
claims.note: Leumit rulebook 0726: surgery with choice of surgeon; 'חוות דעת שניה לבדיקה פתולוגית'; 'בדיקה לגילוי גנים סרטניים לסרטן המעי הגס, סרטן השד וסרטן השחלות'; wig table 'פאה לחולה ... 1,866' (higher tier, 733 lower).

claims.claim: Premiums were obtained for one fund only: Meuhedet Adif at July 2026 runs from 12.24 shekels a month per person under 18 to 92.46 at 70 and over.
claims.note: No Meuhedet source on the card, and no readable Meuhedet price list was found; the 12.24 and 92.46 figures could not be verified.
claims.fixed: Removed the Meuhedet premium sentence; the 'could not establish' card now lists supplementary premiums at all four funds as a gap.

claims.claim: The Adva Center puts supplementary cover at roughly 80 percent of residents, and the Central Bureau of Statistics Social Survey of 2017, quoted by the State Comptroller, found 22 percent of the population holding insurance that covers medicines outside the basket.
claims.note: Adva: 'ומצויים בידי 80% לערך מתושבי ישראל'; Comptroller fn 104: CBS Social Survey 2017, 22% hold insurance for drugs outside the basket.

claims.claim: Household spending on private and supplementary insurance and on co-payments for medicines and treatments reached 15.3 billion shekels in 2020 against 9.6 billion in 2010 at 2020 prices.
claims.note: Adva: 'בשנת 2020 ההוצאה של משקי בית על ביטוחים פרטיים ומשלימים ועל השתתפות בתרופות וטיפולים, עמדה על 15.3 מיליארד ₪. בשנת 2010 ... 9.6 מיליארד ₪ (במחירי 2020)'.

claims.claim: Adva Center, Ministry of Health budget 2023-2024 (Hebrew PDF)
claims.note: Title 'תקציב משרד הבריאות 2023-2024'.

claims.claim: From the OECD's own data, Israeli current health expenditure was 7.089 percent of GDP in 2024, 39th of 50 reporting economies, against Germany 12.2 percent, France 11.3, the United Kingdom 11.1 and Japan 10.3.
claims.note: Current OECD SHA release (SDMX, EXP_HEALTH PT_B1GQ): ISR 2024 6.761 (status D, difference in methodology), DEU 12.208, FRA 11.326, GBR 11.081, JPN 10.447. The page's 7.089 for Israel and 10.3 for Japan come from the superseded archive dataflow; the '39th of 50' rank could not be re-derived.
claims.fixed: Updated to 6.76 percent (flagged by the OECD) and Japan 10.4; dropped the rank; added the current-release query as a link; plain summary now says 'a little under seven percent'.

claims.claim: The 2023 financing mix was government and compulsory schemes 65.24 percent, voluntary schemes 12.83 percent and household out-of-pocket 20.49 percent.
claims.note: Current OECD SHA, ISR 2023 (provisional), share of current health expenditure: HF1 62.691, HF2 11.685, HF3 24.438, against the page's 65.24/12.83/20.49.
claims.fixed: Updated to 62.7, 11.7 and 24.4 percent (provisional); plain summary changed from 'about a fifth' to 'about a quarter' paid directly.

claims.claim: Section 47A of the Pharmacists Ordinance requires the Director to maintain a register of registered preparations and forbids anyone to manufacture, market or direct the use of a preparation unless it is registered and used in accordance with that registration.
claims.note: Ordinance s.47A(a)(1) 'המנהל ינהל פנקס תכשירים רשומים'; (b) 'לא ייצר אדם ולא ישווק תכשיר, ולא יורה על שימוש בו, אלא אם כן הוא תכשיר רשום ובהתאם לרישום'.

claims.claim: The Pharmacists Regulations (Preparations) of 1986 set the procedure.
claims.note: Ordinance note: 'פורסמו תקנות הרוקחים (תכשירים), התשמ"ו–1986'.

claims.claim: For scale, the advisory committee reviewed 620 new-drug and supplemental-indication applications between 2014 and 2019; in the 2014 to 2016 cohort oncology was the largest single field at 31 percent of applications, and oncology applications carried the highest risk of a major label variation after approval.
claims.note: 620 applications 2014-2019 is in Vishkautzan 2026 ('Out of 620 NDAs ... and supplemental indication applications reviewed by the Israeli ACDR between 1 January 2014 and 31 December 2019'), which this card did not cite. Hiayev 2023 (cited): 2014-2016 'oncology (31.0%)' is correct, but it reports an oncologic indication as a significant predictor (HR 2.48) of major variation, not 'the highest risk' (phase II-based approvals HR 2.58).
claims.fixed: Now says an oncology indication independently predicted a major label variation; added Vishkautzan 2026 to the card's links.

claims.claim: Pharmacists Ordinance [New Version] 5741-1981, section 47A (Hebrew)
claims.note: Section 47A present in the consolidated text.

claims.claim: Hiayev et al., Post-approval label variations of drugs approved in Israel following FDA or EMA approval (BMJ Open 2023)
claims.note: Hiayev S et al., BMJ Open 2023, PMC10163499.

claims.claim: Israel recognises eleven jurisdictions, including the United States, the European Union, Japan, Australia and, since 2022, Britain.
claims.note: Regulation 1 'מדינה מוכרת' lists 11 items, (11) בריטניה added by Amendment 5782-2022 of 4 April 2022.

claims.claim: A product identical to one already approved by the FDA or in the EU must be registered within 70 days.
claims.note: s.47A(a2)(2) gives 70 days, but (a2)(3) defines 'תכשיר רפואי – למעט תכשיר ביולוגי ומוצרי דם': biologics, which include many cancer drugs, are outside the 70-day route.
claims.fixed: Added 'unless it is a biological medicine or a blood product'.

claims.claim: The recognised country list sits in regulation 1 of the Pharmacists Regulations: the United States, Canada, any European Union member state, Switzerland, Norway, Iceland, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Israel and, added by amendment in April 2022, Britain.
claims.note: 'מדינה מוכרת – (1) ארצות הברית ... (2) קנדה; (3) ... האיחוד האירופי; (4) שוויץ; (5) נורבגיה; (6) איסלנד; (7) אוסטרליה; (8) ניו זילנד; (9) יפן; (10) ישראל; (11) בריטניה'; amendment Reshumot 10083, 4 April 2022.

claims.claim: Section 47A(a2) of the Ordinance provides that where a preparation is identical to a registered one in active substance, form, strength, route, activity and bioavailability and has been approved for marketing by the FDA or the competent European authority, proof of that approval suffices, and the Director must register it within 70 days or give a reasoned refusal.
claims.note: Conditions and the 70 days are correct ('ירשום המנהל את התכשיר בפנקס בתוך 70 ימים ... אלא אם כן נתן הודעה מנומקת'), but the sentence left out the exclusion of biologics and blood products ('למעט תכשיר ביולוגי ומוצרי דם'), which matters for cancer drugs.
claims.fixed: Added the exclusion of biological products and blood products.

claims.claim: And import approval under regulations 5A and 5B requires certificates from a recognised country.
claims.note: Reg. 5A(b)(5)(a) and 5B(b): 'אישור מרשות מוסמכת במדינה מוכרת'.

claims.claim: The general statutory deadline is 270 days from submission, with a stop-clock while the applicant completes the file.
claims.note: Reg. 5(ז) 'בתוך 270 ימים מיום הגשת הבקשה'; 5(ח) time for additional data is added.

claims.claim: Pharmacists Regulations (Preparations) (Amendment) 5782-2022, adding Britain to the recognised countries (Hebrew PDF)
claims.note: Reshumot 10083, 'תקנות הרוקחים (תכשירים) (תיקון), התשפ"ב-2022', 4 April 2022.

claims.claim: Vishkautzan et al., Post-approval safety label variations for drugs approved in Israel 2014-2019 (BMJ Open 2026)
claims.note: Vishkautzan A et al., BMJ Open 2026, 2014-2019 ACDR cohort.

claims.claim: Registration sits under section 47A of the Pharmacists Ordinance; funding sits under sections 8 and 9 of the National Health Insurance Law.
claims.note: Ordinance s.47A (register); NHI Law s.8 (the basket, 8(e) funding condition) and s.9 (cost update).

claims.claim: The only quantification that could be found is a proxy: of 3,284 compassionate treatments between 2020 and 2024, 60 percent of the commonest technologies, 13 of 22, were later included in the basket, typically after more than two years of compassionate use.
claims.note: Schwartzberg 2025: 3,284 treatments; '60% of the most common technologies (13 out of 22) were subsequently included ... exceeded two years'.

claims.claim: Schwartzberg et al., Compassionate use in Israel 2020-2024 (Isr J Health Policy Res 2025)
Director's consent under the Pharmacists Regulations, Reshumot 7348, 20 September 2016 (Hebrew PDF)
claims.note: Footnote: 'י"פ 7348, התשע"ו (20.9.2016)'.

claims.claim: The Ministry's procedure sets the clock at 60 working days.
claims.note: Procedure 14-3: 'החלטה ... תינתן תוך 60 ימי עבודה' (central/Supreme committee route).

claims.claim: The Public Health Regulations (Medical Experiments on Human Subjects) of 1980 forbid a medical trial on a human in a hospital without written approval, subject to the Declaration of Helsinki, which is annexed to them.
claims.note: Regulations dated 'ד׳ בחשון התשמ״א (14 באוקטובר 1980)'; approval requires the hospital Helsinki committee's written notice and conformity with the Helsinki Declaration.

claims.claim: Regulation 3B requires the opinion of the Supreme Helsinki Committee, a ten-member national body including two public members and six professors, for any trial touching a person's genetic makeup, any trial involving non-natural fertilisation, and anything else the Director refers.
claims.note: Reg. 3B: '(1) ניסוי הנוגע למערך הגנטי של אדם; (2) ... להפריית אשה שלא בדרך הטבע; (3) ענין אחר שהמנהל ...'; Third Schedule: 'מנינה: עשרה חברים ובהם – (1) שני אנשי ציבור ... (2) ששה פרופסורים'.

claims.claim: The Ministry's Procedure 14, in force since May 2020, classifies a complete application as special or not within two working days, requires material 15 working days before a meeting and 30 where a quality dossier is assessed, and sets decisions at 60 working days through the central and Supreme Committee route, 45 through the expert-opinion route and 30 for professional handling within the clinical trials department, excluding time waiting for the applicant.
claims.note: Procedure 14-3/02 'תחולת הנוהל – 01/05/2020'; 'יסווג ... בתוך 2 ימי עבודה'; '15 ימי עבודה לפני הדיון ... תיק האיכות 30 ימי עבודה'; 60/45/30 working days; 'זמן ההמתנה להשלמות אינו נכלל'.

claims.claim: Public Health Regulations (Medical Experiments on Human Subjects) 5741-1980, consolidated Hebrew text
claims.note: Consolidated text of the 1980 regulations.

claims.claim: Ministry of Health Procedure 14, chapter 1: operation of Helsinki committees (Hebrew PDF)
claims.note: Procedure 14 chapter 1 PDF, in force 01/05/2020.

claims.claim: Ministry of Health Procedure 14, chapter 3: new trial applications (Hebrew PDF)
claims.note: Procedure 14-3/02, new trial applications.

claims.claim: Neuhausen and colleagues demonstrated this for BRCA1 in 1996 across 61 families;
claims.note: Correct, but the paper was not linked. Neuhausen SL et al., Am J Hum Genet 1996 (PMID 8571953, PMC1914544): 'we constructed a haplotype of nine polymorphic markers ... in a set of 61 breast/ovarian cancer families selected for having one of six recurrent BRCA1 mutations'.
claims.fixed: Added Neuhausen et al. 1996 to the card's links.

claims.claim: Laitman and colleagues dated BRCA1 c.68_69delAG to roughly 750 to 1,500 years ago, while Bar-Sade and colleagues had argued from its presence in Iraqi and Moroccan Jewish communities that it predates the diaspora.
claims.note: Laitman 2013: 'Haplotype analysis indicated that the 185delAG mutation arose 750-1500 years ago'. Bar-Sade 1998: Iraqi Jews (previous study) and Moroccan carriers; title 'originated before the dispersion of Jews in the diaspora'.

claims.claim: The practical point is arithmetic: where three variants account for about 90 percent of the BRCA alterations found in a population, a three-variant panel does most of the work of full sequencing at a fraction of the cost.
claims.note: Ahmad 2023: 'the three BRCA founder variants which account for approximately 90% of identified BRCA alterations'.

claims.claim: Ahmad et al., Founder variants and population genomes (Hereditary Cancer in Clinical Practice 2023)
claims.note: DOI 10.1186/s13053-023-00256-2 resolves to Ahmad O et al., 'BRCA1/2 potential founder variants in the Jordanian population: an opportunity for a customized screening panel'. The label's title 'Founder variants and population genomes' does not exist. Right paper, wrong title.
claims.fixed: Label corrected to the paper's real subject (Jordanian founder variants, with a review of the founder effect).

claims.claim: Laitman et al., Haplotype analysis of BRCA1 c.68_69delAG across eleven populations (Eur J Hum Genet 2013)
claims.note: DOI resolves to Laitman Y et al., 'Haplotype analysis of the 185delAG BRCA1 mutation in ethnically diverse populations', EJHG 2013 (eleven groups listed).

claims.claim: Bar-Sade et al., The 185delAG BRCA1 mutation originated before the dispersion of Jews in the diaspora (Hum Mol Genet 1998)
claims.note: Bar-Sade RB et al., Hum Mol Genet 1998, title matches.

claims.claim: Three specific changes in BRCA1 and BRCA2 are carried by about one in 46 Ashkenazi Jews.
claims.note: Gabai-Kapara: '2.17% (178/8195) for the three alleles combined' = 1 in 46.

claims.claim: The Israeli study that made testing everyone defensible did something unusual: it found carriers among 8,195 healthy men, then followed their female relatives, so the risk figures did not come from families already known to cancer clinics.
claims.note: 'DNA samples from 8,195 subjects (99.7%) were successfully genotyped'; female relatives of carriers then enrolled.

claims.claim: The three are BRCA1 c.68_69delAG (185delAG), identified by Struewing and colleagues in 1995 at 0.9 percent in 858 Ashkenazi people seeking testing for unrelated conditions;
claims.note: Correct, but the 1995 paper was not linked. Struewing JP et al., Nat Genet 1995 (10.1038/ng1095-198): '858 Ashkenazim seeking genetic testing for conditions unrelated to cancer'. Oddoux 1996: 'The 185delAG mutation was observed in 0.9% of 858 Ashkenazi Jews'.
claims.fixed: Added Struewing et al. 1995 to the card's links.

claims.claim: BRCA1 c.5266dupC (5382insC), at 0.13 percent in about 3,000 unselected Ashkenazi samples in Roa and colleagues' 1996 study; and BRCA2 c.5946delT (6174delT), at about 1 percent in 1,255 Jewish individuals in Oddoux and colleagues' work and 1.52 percent in Roa's 3,085.
claims.note: Roa 1996 (linked): '5382insC ... 0.13%' in ~3,000; '6174delT ... 1.52%' in 3,085. Oddoux 1996, not linked: 'population survey of 1,255 Jewish individuals ... prevalence of approximately 1%'.
claims.fixed: Added Oddoux et al. 1996 to the card's links.

claims.claim: Struewing's 1997 New England Journal study of 5,318 Jewish volunteers in Washington found 120 carriers, 2.26 percent.
claims.note: Struewing 1997: 'blood samples from 5318 Jewish subjects' (Washington, D.C. area); 'One hundred twenty carriers' = 2.26%.

claims.claim: The Israeli population cohort is the one that changed policy: Gabai-Kapara, Levy-Lahad, Mary-Claire King and colleagues genotyped 8,195 healthy Ashkenazi Israeli men recruited from health-screening centres between 2004 and 2010, found 2.17 percent carrying one of the three, then enrolled their female relatives.
claims.note: 'recruited between June 2004 and December 2010'; 8,195 genotyped; '2.17% (178/8195) for the three alleles combined'.

claims.claim: Cumulative risk of breast or ovarian cancer by age 80 was 0.83 for BRCA1 carriers and 0.76 for BRCA2 carriers, and age-specific risk was 3.8-fold higher for carriers born after 1958.
claims.note: 'by age 60 and 80 ... 0.83 (± 0.07) for BRCA1 ... 0.76 (± 0.13) for BRCA2'; 'Age-specific cancer risks ... were 3.8-fold higher for carriers in the younger vs. the older birth cohort' (born after 1958).

claims.claim: The paper also states that in the Ashkenazi Jewish population of Israel 11 percent of breast cancer and 40 percent of ovarian cancer are due to these three variants.
claims.note: Abstract: 'In the Ashkenazi Jewish (AJ) population of Israel, 11% of breast cancer and 40% of ovarian cancer are due to three inherited founder mutations'.

claims.claim: The number that settled the argument is that 51 percent of the 167 carrier families had little or no relevant cancer history, and only 35 percent of the high-burden families had ever been referred for genetic counselling, in a country with universal coverage.
claims.note: '51% (85 of 167) families ... had little or no history of relevant cancer'; 'only 35% (29 of 82) of high-cancer-incidence families had been referred previously for genetic counseling'.

claims.claim: Compare the large clinic-ascertained prospective cohort of Kuchenbaecker and colleagues, 94 percent recruited through family clinics, which gives breast cancer risk to 80 of 72 percent for BRCA1 and 69 percent for BRCA2: the difference in ascertainment is the whole point.
claims.note: Kuchenbaecker: 'ascertainment through family clinics (94%)'; 'cumulative breast cancer risk to age 80 years was 72% ... for BRCA1 and 69% ... for BRCA2'.

claims.claim: Gabai-Kapara et al., Population-based screening for breast and ovarian cancer risk due to BRCA1 and BRCA2 (PNAS 2014)
claims.note: Gabai-Kapara E et al., PNAS 2014.

claims.claim: Struewing et al., The risk of cancer associated with specific mutations of BRCA1 and BRCA2 among Ashkenazi Jews (NEJM 1997)
claims.note: Struewing JP et al., NEJM 1997.

claims.claim: Roa et al., Ashkenazi Jewish population frequencies for common mutations in BRCA1 and BRCA2 (Nat Genet 1996)
claims.note: Roa BB et al., Nat Genet 1996.

claims.claim: Kuchenbaecker et al., Risks of breast, ovarian and contralateral breast cancer for BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutation carriers (JAMA 2017)
claims.note: Kuchenbaecker KB et al., JAMA 2017.

claims.claim: Since January 2020 any woman in Israel who says she is of Ashkenazi origin can have the three-variant test free, once in her life, with no family history needed and no requirement to see a genetic counsellor first.
claims.note: The circular of 28 January 2020 covers 'בדיקת סקר למוטציות שכיחות בגנים BRCA1/BRCA2' for every woman of Ashkenazi origin by self-declaration. It does not specify three variants, and Clalit screened 14 ('screened for 14 pathogenic variants in BRCA1/2', Greenberg 2023). 'Three-variant test' is not accurate.
claims.fixed: 'three-variant test' changed to 'founder-variant test'.

claims.claim: About 165,000 women were tested between mid-2021 and 2024, of whom about 2,350 were carriers.
claims.note: Michaelson-Cohen 2026: 'From mid-2021 through 2024, approximately 2,350 of 165,000 (1.42%) women tested via PS were identified as carriers'.

claims.claim: The entitlement arrived through the ordinary basket mechanism, in Ministry of Health circular 3/2020 of 28 January 2020, the annual basket expansion circular.
claims.note: Circular 'מס' 3/2020', '28 ינואר 2020', 'הרחבת סל שירותי הבריאות לשנת 2020'.

claims.claim: From mid-2021 through 2024 about 2,350 of 165,000 women tested through population screening, 1.42 percent, were carriers, roughly 650 a year.
claims.note: 'approximately 2,350 of 165,000 (1.42%) ... (~ 650 annually)'.

claims.claim: Clalit's own published evaluation of the first two years found 120 pathogenic variants in 13,502 Ashkenazi Jewish women screened between June 2020 and June 2022, 0.89 percent, with the three founder variants accounting for 96.6 percent of those found, and women who came forward younger and of higher socioeconomic status than eligible women who did not.
claims.note: Greenberg 2023: '13,502 women ... between June 2020 and June 2022 ... 0.89% (120 of 13,502) ... Three variants ... accounted for 96.6% ... tested women were younger and of a higher socioeconomic status'.

claims.claim: A real-world comparison at Shaare Zedek of 352 newly identified unaffected carriers found that those coming through population screening more often carried BRCA2, 62.9 against 48.7 percent, and less often had a suggestive family history, 40.4 against 61 percent, and reported lower satisfaction with how the result was delivered, but testing route did not predict psychosocial outcomes on multivariate analysis and risk-reducing surgery rates at the recommended age were similar.
claims.note: Armon 2026: '352 carriers'; 'BRCA2-PVs (62.9% v 48.7%)'; 'suggestive family history (FH) (40.4% v 61%)'; lower satisfaction with result delivery; 'testing mode was not predictive of psychosocial outcomes in multivariate analysis'; RR-BSO at recommended age similar.

claims.claim: Since the programme the nine high-risk clinics have agreed one national protocol: annual MRI from 25, mammography added from 30, risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy at 35 to 40 for BRCA1 carriers and 40 to 45 for BRCA2, and pancreatic surveillance from 50 for BRCA2.
claims.note: Michaelson-Cohen 2026, nine HRSCs, consortium Table 2: annual MRI from 25; from 30 MRI with 'MG at 6-month intervals'; RRSO 'BRCA1: ages 35-40. BRCA2: ages 40-45'; pancreatic surveillance BRCA2 'consider for all carriers from age 50'.

claims.claim: Not everyone is happy: in a survey of Israeli clinical geneticists and counsellors, most felt carriers did not fully understand the implications of a positive result when consenting, and 8 of 28 had initially opposed the programme.
claims.note: Furman 2025: 'most carriers did not comprehend the implications of a positive result'; 'Eight survey participants (29%) reported they were initially against the screening program' (about 28 respondents).

claims.claim: Michaelson-Cohen et al., Managing healthcare for female BRCA carriers in the population screening era (Isr J Health Policy Res 2026)
claims.note: Michaelson-Cohen R et al., Isr J Health Policy Res 2026.

claims.claim: Ministry of Health circular 3/2020, expansion of the health services basket for 2020 (Hebrew PDF)
claims.note: Circular 3/2020, 2020 basket expansion.

claims.claim: Greenberg et al., the first two years of national BRCA screening at Clalit (Genetics in Medicine Open 2023)
claims.note: Greenberg R et al., Genetics in Medicine Open 2023; Clalit authors (Balicer, Ben-Shachar).

claims.claim: Armon et al., population screening versus oncogenetic clinics (JCO Precision Oncology 2026)
claims.note: Armon S et al., JCO Precision Oncology 2026.

claims.claim: Furman et al., Israeli genetics professionals on the population screening programme (Breast Care 2025)
claims.note: Furman Y et al., Breast Care 2025.

claims.claim: The programme has begun to widen: the Israel Cancer Association reports that from September 2025 women of Ethiopian descent became eligible too.
claims.note: No source on the card supported the date. The ICA annual report 2025 (cited elsewhere on the page) says only 'BRCA screening extended to women of Ethiopian descent' under October 2025 activities, with no date. A Maariv item found by search gives September 2025, but it was not read in raw text and is not cited.
claims.fixed: Now 'in 2025 screening was extended to women of Ethiopian descent'; ICA annual report added to the card's links.

claims.claim: The Israeli survey of high-risk families found community-specific recurring variants: BRCA1 Tyr978X in 23 of 892 people of Iraqi and Iranian Jewish origin, 2.6 percent;
claims.note: Laitman 2012: 'Tyr978X ... 23/892, 2.6% of the Asians tested' (Iraq and Iran).

claims.claim: BRCA1 c.981delAT in 7 of 264 of North African Jewish origin, 2.65 percent;
claims.note: 'Of North Africans, 7/264 (2.65%) carried the BRCA1*981delAT mutation'.

claims.claim: BRCA1 A1708E in 8 of 282 and BRCA2 R2336P in 4 of 180 of Balkan Jewish origin.
claims.note: '8/282 (2.8%) of the Balkan cases carried the BRCA1*A1708E mutation, 4/180 (2.2%) the R2336P'.

claims.claim: Among Ethiopian Jews, three recurrent BRCA2 variants were found in 11 breast cancer patients whose mean age at diagnosis was 35.7, with a combined carrier rate in controls of 1.8 percent, 5 of 280, an order comparable with the Ashkenazi figure; the authors called for a culturally adapted screening approach, and the Israel Cancer Association reports that on 1 September 2025 BRCA testing entered the basket for women of Ethiopian descent as well, putting about a million Israeli women in scope, of whom it estimates 42,000 to 47,000 are of Ethiopian descent.
claims.note: Lieberman 2022 is correct: 'three recurrent BRCA2 PVs in 11 EJ breast cancer patients'; 'mean age at diagnosis was 35.7y'; 'Combined carrier rate among controls was 1.8% (5/280)'; 'culturally adapted population screening approach'. The ICA claims ('1 September 2025', 'about a million', '42,000 to 47,000') are on no linked source; the ICA annual report gives no date or numbers.
claims.fixed: Replaced the unsourced date and numbers with what the ICA 2025 report states (screening extended to women of Ethiopian descent).

claims.claim: In 188 consecutive Israeli Arab breast and ovarian cancer patients, 10 percent carried one of 12 pathogenic variants, with detection reaching 32 percent among the ovarian cancer patients; among 68 high-risk Druze, Muslim Arab and Christian Arab families, panel sequencing found only three pathogenic variants and 29 of uncertain significance.
claims.note: Bernstein-Molho 2019 is correct: '188 patients ... 18 (10%) carried one of 12 pathogenic or likely-pathogenic variants ... Of patients with ovarian cancer, 12/38 (32%) were carriers'. The '68 high-risk Druze, Muslim Arab and Christian Arab families ... three pathogenic variants and 29 VUS' clause matches no linked source (Laitman 2011 had 45 Moslem, 21 Christian Arab and 17 Druze women, with 8 pathogenic carriers).
claims.fixed: Removed the unsourced 68-family clause.

claims.claim: Mary-Claire King's Palestinian work found something different again: in 875 women with invasive breast cancer, TP53 p.R181C was the single most frequent variant, responsible for 15 percent of cancers among young-onset or familial patients, and the later risk estimate was 50 percent by age 50 and 81 percent by 80 with, importantly, no excess of paediatric cancer in relatives, so the phenotype is narrower than textbook Li-Fraumeni syndrome and testing children of these families is unwarranted.
claims.note: Int J Cancer 2017: '875 Palestinian patients with invasive breast cancer'; 'TP53 p.R181C ... responsible for 15% of breast cancers among young onset or familial patients'. JNCI 2025: '50% by age 50 years and 81% by age 80 years'; paediatric cancer in relatives OR 0.90; 'genetic testing in children is unwarranted'.

claims.claim: The decisive Israeli finding for policy is the negative one: across 250 ethnically diverse high-risk Israeli families screened after the common Jewish founders were excluded, 19 different pathogenic BRCA1/2 variants turned up and none recurred often enough to panel for.
claims.note: Laitman 2011: '250 high risk ... All Jewish women were prescreened'; '22 (8.8%) participants carried 19 clearly pathogenic mutations'; 'no predominant recurring germline mutations'.

claims.claim: There is also a geographic gap: a survey of every Israeli public hospital found ten dedicated multidisciplinary carrier clinics following about 4,500 carriers, with none in the southern district or the northern half of the northern district.
claims.note: No source on the card. Michaelson-Cohen 2026 says the national survey 'identified nine clinics managing approximately 4,500 BRCA-PVCs', not ten. The southern district and northern-half gap is in no source read.
claims.fixed: Now: a national survey identified nine dedicated carrier clinics following about 4,500 carriers; the unsourced geography was removed; Michaelson-Cohen 2026 added to the card's links.

claims.claim: Laitman et al., Recurring founder mutations in BRCA1 and BRCA2 in ethnically diverse Jewish populations (Breast Cancer Res Treat 2012)
claims.note: DOI 10.1007/s10549-012-2006-8 is titled 'Recurrent germline mutations in BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes in high risk families in Israel'; the label's title was invented. Right paper.
claims.fixed: Label corrected to the real title.

claims.claim: Lieberman et al., Recurrent BRCA2 variants in Ethiopian Jewish breast cancer patients (Breast Cancer Res Treat 2022)
claims.note: DOI 10.1007/s10549-022-06557-9 is titled 'Common founder BRCA2 pathogenic variants and breast cancer characteristics in Ethiopian Jews'. Right paper, invented title.
claims.fixed: Label corrected to the real title.

claims.claim: Bernstein-Molho et al., Germline pathogenic variants in Israeli Arab breast and ovarian cancer patients (Breast Cancer Res Treat 2019)
claims.note: DOI 10.1007/s10549-019-05379-6 is titled 'The yield of full BRCA1/2 genotyping in Israeli Arab high-risk breast/ovarian cancer patients'. Right paper, invented title.
claims.fixed: Label corrected to the real title.

claims.claim: Lolas Hamameh et al., Genomic analysis of inherited breast cancer among Palestinian women (Int J Cancer 2017)
claims.note: Lolas Hamameh S et al., Int J Cancer 2017, title matches (shortened).

claims.claim: Lolas-Hamameh et al., Cancer risks for TP53 p.R181C heterozygotes (JNCI 2025)
claims.note: DOI 10.1093/jnci/djae334 is titled 'TP53 missense allele predisposing to high risk of breast cancer but not pediatric cancers'; the label paraphrased it as if it were the title.
claims.fixed: Label corrected to the real title.

claims.claim: Laitman et al., No predominant recurring germline mutations among ethnically diverse Israeli high-risk families (Breast Cancer Res Treat 2011)
claims.note: DOI 10.1007/s10549-010-1217-0 is titled 'Germline mutations in BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes in ethnically diverse high risk families in Israel'. The label took a phrase from the conclusion and used it as the title.
claims.fixed: Label corrected to the real title.

claims.claim: About one in fifteen Ashkenazi Jews carries a change in the APC gene called I1307K.
claims.note: Laken: 'found in 6% of Ashkenazi Jews'; UK Biobank: '7.1% of AJ'; 1 in 15 = 6.7%.

claims.claim: Laken and colleagues identified APC c.3920T>A (p.Ile1307Lys) in 1997, finding it in 6 percent of Ashkenazi Jews and about 28 percent of those with a family history of colorectal cancer, and showed the mechanism: the change converts the sequence into an eight-adenine homopolymer tract prone to somatic truncating mutation.
claims.note: Laken 1997: 'T to A at APC nucleotide 3920 found in 6% of Ashkenazi Jews and about 28% of Ashkenazim with a family history of CRC ... creates a small hypermutable region'. The A8 tract detail is the paper's mechanism (abstract read).

claims.claim: The InSiGHT position statement of 2023, from a systematic review of 65 papers, records a gnomAD minor allele frequency of 3.6 percent in Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry against under 0.15 percent in European, Asian, Latino or African populations, and about 2.5 percent in Sephardi Jewish individuals; it classifies the variant as pathogenic with low penetrance, a risk factor in people of Ashkenazi Jewish origin who should be tested and offered surveillance, with insufficient evidence in other populations.
claims.note: InSiGHT 2023 full text: '65 articles were included'; 'MAF gnomAD =3.6%'; '~2.5% of Sephardi Jewish'; '<0.15% in European, Asian, Latino or African populations'; 'pathogenic, low penetrance ... should be tested in this population ... not enough evidence ... other populations'.

claims.claim: The commonly quoted odds ratio of 1.7 to 1.8 is now contested.
claims.note: Allen 2025: 'The previously established OR of 1.7-1.8 for AJ individuals'.

claims.claim: A UK Biobank analysis of 466,315 people with 8,944 colorectal cancers found no significant association in Ashkenazi Jewish participants, odds ratio 0.71, and noted that the established estimate lies inside its own confidence interval, so the study was underpowered rather than contradictory.
claims.note: '466 315 individuals (8944 with CRC)'; 'AJ (OR: 0.71; 95% CI: 0.17 to 2.95)'; 'lies within our 95% CI, indicating underpowered results'.

claims.claim: A large Israeli prospective screening cohort of 13,013 healthy subjects found the variant in 11.8 percent of cancer patients against 4.7 percent of healthy subjects, an adjusted odds ratio of 2.53.
claims.note: Leshno 2016: '13,013 healthy subjects ... supplemented with 1,611 cancer patients from the same institution ... detected in 189 (11.8%) cancer patients compared to 614 (4.7%) healthy subjects ... OR 2.53'. The sentence implied the cancer patients came from the healthy screening cohort, and left out that the OR is for any cancer.
claims.fixed: Now names the two groups (13,013 healthy subjects and 1,611 cancer patients) and says the odds ratio is for cancer of any type.

claims.claim: It is not in the national programme, whose 2020 circular covers BRCA1 and BRCA2 only; it is tested clinically on Israeli founder panels, where one study found that of 128 people carrying at least one panel variant, 84 carried a low-penetrance variant unrelated to the cancer they had been diagnosed with.
claims.note: The 2020 circular covering BRCA1/2 only is correct (circular 3/2020). The founder-panel study (128 carriers, 84 low-penetrance) is on no linked source and could not be identified.
claims.fixed: Removed the unsourced founder-panel clause.

claims.claim: Laken et al., Familial colorectal cancer in Ashkenazim due to a hypermutable tract in APC (Nat Genet 1997)
claims.note: Laken SJ et al., Nat Genet 1997, title matches.

claims.claim: Valle, Katz et al., InSiGHT position statement on APC I1307K (J Med Genet 2023)
claims.note: Valle L, Katz LH et al., J Med Genet 2023.

claims.claim: Allen et al., APC I1307K and colorectal cancer risk in UK Biobank (J Med Genet 2025)
claims.note: Allen S et al., J Med Genet 2025.

claims.claim: Leshno et al., APC I1307K in a prospective Israeli screening cohort (Int J Cancer 2016)
claims.note: Leshno A et al., Int J Cancer 2016.

claims.claim: What knowing changes: PARP inhibitors, surveillance, and a trial that had to screen 3,315 people
claims.note: POLO NEJM 2019: 'Of the 3315 patients who underwent screening, 154 underwent randomization'.

claims.claim: It had to screen 3,315 patients to randomise 154, which is the argument for knowing before you need to know.
claims.note: 3,315 screened, 154 randomised.

claims.claim: Talia Golan of Sheba Medical Center led POLO, a randomised placebo-controlled phase 3 of maintenance olaparib in metastatic pancreatic cancer with a germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation whose disease had not progressed on first-line platinum.
claims.note: Golan T first author; 'randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 ... germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation and metastatic pancreatic cancer and disease that had not progressed during first-line platinum-based chemotherapy'.

claims.claim: Median progression-free survival was 7.4 months against 3.8, hazard ratio 0.53.
claims.note: '7.4 months vs. 3.8 months; hazard ratio ... 0.53'.

claims.claim: The final overall survival analysis found no significant difference in medians, 19.0 against 19.2 months, but the curves separated late, with estimated three-year survival of 33.9 percent against 17.8 percent.
claims.note: JCO 2022: 'median 19.0 v 19.2 months; HR 0.83 ... Kaplan-Meier OS curves separated at approximately 24 months ... 3-year survival ... 33.9% versus 17.8%'.

claims.claim: The screening ratio, 3,315 screened for 154 randomised, is the practical case for population-level knowledge of carrier status rather than testing at the point of need.
claims.note: 3315/154 as above.

claims.claim: Downstream of that, Israel runs pancreatic surveillance in BRCA carriers and has published outcomes: in a multicentre cohort of 180 asymptomatic carriers followed a median four years, four adenocarcinomas and four grade 1 neuroendocrine tumours were found, all in BRCA2 carriers, two of them with no family history of pancreatic cancer, and three of the four cancers were resectable; a second Israeli prospective cohort of 239 high-risk people found pancreatic cancer in 11, 73 percent at an early stage.
claims.note: Laish 2024: '180 asymptomatic carriers ... median follow-up period of 4 years ... four cases of adenocarcinoma and four cases of grade 1-neuroendocrine tumor ... All were BRCA2 carriers, and two had no family history ... Three cancer patients were at resectable stages'. Rosner 2024: '239 HRIs ... PDAC was detected in 11 individuals (4.6%), with 73% diagnosed at an early stage'.

claims.claim: Breast surveillance changes stage too: in a Sheba cohort of 298 carriers, 19.8 percent of those who knew their status and were under surveillance presented with carcinoma in situ, against 5 percent of those who learned their status only after diagnosis.
claims.note: Correct, but the source was not linked. Bernstein-Molho et al., Breast 2020 (10.1016/j.breast.2019.10.012, Sheba): 'Data were available for 298 BRCA1/2 carriers ... Of known carriers, 19.8% were diagnosed with carcinoma in situ vs. 5% of latent carriers'.
claims.fixed: Added Bernstein-Molho et al. 2020 to the card's links.

claims.claim: Golan et al., Maintenance olaparib for germline BRCA-mutated metastatic pancreatic cancer (NEJM 2019)
claims.note: Golan T et al., NEJM 2019.

claims.claim: Golan et al., POLO final overall survival (J Clin Oncol 2022)
claims.note: DOI 10.1200/JCO.21.01604 lists Kindler HL as first author, not Golan.
claims.fixed: Label changed to 'Kindler et al.'.

claims.claim: Laish et al., Pancreatic surveillance in Israeli BRCA1/2 carriers (Cancer 2024)
claims.note: Laish I et al., Cancer 2024, Israeli multicentre BRCA cohort (descriptive label).

claims.claim: Rosner et al., Six years of pancreatic surveillance in 239 Israeli high-risk individuals (Clin Transl Gastroenterol 2024)
claims.note: Rosner G et al., CTG 2024, 239 HRIs, 6-year prospective surveillance (descriptive label).

claims.claim: On phase 1 cancer trials per million people it sits fourth in the world, behind Australia, Denmark and Belgium.
claims.note: Re-run on 3 Nov 2026, recruiting phase 1 cancer studies per million (World Bank 2024): Australia 374/27.19m=13.8, Denmark 66/5.98m=11.0, Belgium 100/11.86m=8.4, Israel 83/10.00m=8.3; Singapore, Spain, Netherlands, US, Switzerland (5.2), Korea (5.0), Taiwan (~5.9) and others are lower. Only Monaco (1 study) is higher, a micro-state artefact.

claims.claim: Counted against the ClinicalTrials.gov API on 25 September 2026, using a country filter rather than a free-text location search, Israel has 2,255 registered cancer studies of any status, 318 recruiting, and 82 recruiting at phase 1.
claims.note: Re-run 3 Nov 2026: 2,270 any status, 322 recruiting, 83 recruiting phase 1, against 2,255/318/82 on 25 Sep 2026. The small difference is registry drift; the page dates its count.

claims.claim: That is 2.19 percent of the world's 3,741 recruiting phase 1 cancer studies and 1.69 percent of the 18,860 recruiting at all phases, from about 0.12 percent of world population.

Per million people, using World Bank 2024 populations, phase 1 recruiting cancer trials run 13.42 in Australia, 11.04 in Denmark, 8.35 in Belgium, 8.20 in Israel, 7.45 in Singapore, 7.31 in Spain, 6.34 in the Netherlands and 5.92 in the United States.
claims.note: With World Bank 2024 populations, the stated rates imply 365, 66, 99, 82, 45, 357, 114 and 2,013 studies; re-run counts are 374, 66, 100, 83, 44, 358, 114 and 2,014. Consistent.

claims.claim: The caveat is worth printing because it is where most inflated Israeli trial figures come from: the loose location search returns 119 phase 1 recruiting cancer studies rather than 82, and 37 of those have no Israeli site at all, most of them at Beth Israel hospitals in the United States.
claims.note: Re-run: query.locn=Israel gives 120 recruiting phase 1 cancer studies; 37 have no Israeli site, of which 36 list Beth Israel.

claims.claim: Six centres do most of the work; of the 82 phase 1 studies, Sheba appears in 51, Rambam 45, Hadassah 37, Rabin and Davidoff 31, Tel Aviv Sourasky 25 and Shaare Zedek 12.
claims.note: Re-run on 83 studies by facility-name matching: Sheba 56, Rambam 44, Hadassah 35, Rabin/Davidoff 33, Sourasky 27, Shaare Zedek 11. That ordering and scale agree with the page's 25 Sep counts (51/45/37/31/25/12); exact numbers depend on the matching and on drift.

claims.claim: Sixty-eight of the 82 are industry-sponsored, and eleven have sites only in Israel, which is domestic investigator-initiated early-phase work rather than site participation.
claims.note: Re-run: 69 of 83 have an INDUSTRY lead sponsor and 11 have Israeli sites only (page: 68 of 82, 11).

claims.claim: One honest line about the trend: Israel's share of world phase 1 oncology starts fell from 2.59 percent in 2022 to 2.03 in 2023 and 1.60 in 2024 before recovering to 2.07 in 2025, while world starts stayed flat, so the dip is specific to Israel and coincides with the war from October 2023.
claims.note: Re-run, phase 1 cancer studies by start year, Israel/world: 2022 37/1429 = 2.59%; 2023 28/1376 = 2.03%; 2024 23/1379 = 1.67%; 2025 30/1398 = 2.15%. 2022-23 match exactly; 2024-25 drift up slightly with late registrations. World starts flat.

claims.claim: Clalit's research institute describes an electronic health record database of comprehensive clinical and administrative data since 2000, with some records to the early 1990s, covering the 4.7 million patients the NEJM paper on its COVID vaccine cohort described as 53 percent of the population; its own public pages give the span variously as 20, 26 and 30 years, so the honest phrasing is decades rather than a number.
claims.note: NEJM (Dagan 2021): 'insures 4.7 million patients (53% of the population)' is correct. The archived Clalit page describes a centralised warehouse of 'clinical and administrative data from the majority of medical encounters' but gives no 'since 2000', 'early 1990s' or '20, 26 and 30 years'.
claims.fixed: Removed the unsourced dates and the span comparison; kept what the archived page and the NEJM paper state.

claims.claim: Maccabi's KSM Research and Innovation Center, founded in 2016, reports 2.7 million members, a million biobank samples and 54 partners, with cancer a standing disease registry; its published oncology work includes a breast cancer short-term risk model built on 1,039,212 members and 18,959 diagnoses with an area under the curve of 0.85 for diagnosis within a year, and the external validation and routine deployment of prostate biopsy AI across 11,429 slides.
claims.note: Feinstein 2025: '1,039,212 members ... 18,959 people were diagnosed ... AUC-ROC of 0.85' (one-year prediction) is correct. Pantanowitz 2020: 'used to assess 11 429 H&E-stained slides' in routine deployment is correct. KSM 'founded in 2016', '2.7 million members, a million biobank samples and 54 partners' are on no linked source.
claims.fixed: Removed the unsourced KSM figures.

claims.claim: Leumit's research institute works on about 730,000 members and two decades of data.
claims.note: No Leumit source on the card for 730,000 members or two decades of data.
claims.fixed: Removed the sentence.

claims.claim: The often-repeated claim that Pfizer bought Israel's individual patient records for vaccine data is wrong and worth correcting: the January 2021 agreement with the Ministry of Health provides for weekly aggregate national surveillance counts, and the famous individual-level study of 596,618 matched pairs was a separate Clalit analysis carrying no Pfizer funding statement.
claims.note: Rosen et al. 2021: the January 2021 MOH-Pfizer agreement concerned 'the collection, sharing, and analysis of aggregate, real-world epidemiological data'. 'Weekly' is not in the source. Dagan 2021: 'Each study group included 596,618 persons', a Clalit analysis.
claims.fixed: 'weekly aggregate national surveillance counts' changed to 'aggregate national epidemiological data'.

claims.claim: Clalit Research Institute, about and data governance (archived 2024)
claims.note: Archived 25 February 2024 snapshot of the Clalit Research Institute data page.
